function.summary: Opens in systole and closes in diastole (P2), at about a fifth of systemic pressure.
function.detail: P2 normally follows A2. Inspiration fills the RV more, so it empties later and P2 moves away from A2 (physiological splitting).

supply.summary: No vessels of importance; the RVOT around it is fed by the conus branch.
supply.detail: Conus branch from the RCA (or its own ostium) and LAD branches.

relations.why: Behind and to the right: the outflow tracts cross.
Runs just behind the pulmonary trunk.
The patient's own pulmonary valve can replace a diseased aortic valve; a homograft takes its place.

echo.text: Beyond the RVOT, upper right of the image; Doppler for stenosis and regurgitation.

cut.text: At the top of the RVOT.
The front valve of the base.

ecg.text: Significant stenosis: RV hypertrophy (right axis, dominant R in V1).

complications.name: Pulmonary stenosis
complications.mechanism: Fused or dysplastic cusps (congenital; Noonan) block RV outflow; the RV thickens.
complications.presentation: Ejection click and murmur at the left upper sternal edge, RVH; severe cases cause exertional breathlessness.

complications.name: Regurgitation after Fallot repair
complications.mechanism: Repair opens up the valve area, so it leaks; the RV dilates over years.
complications.presentation: Exercise intolerance, VT, RV dilation on CMR.

complications.name: Pulmonary hypertension
complications.mechanism: The valve is normal, but high pressure dilates the trunk and ring.
complications.presentation: Loud P2, early diastolic pulmonary regurgitation murmur (Graham Steell), RV failure.

complications.name: Carcinoid heart disease
complications.mechanism: Serotonin plaques stiffen the cusps.
complications.presentation: Pulmonary stenosis and regurgitation alongside TR.

student.text: Inspiration sends more blood to the right heart, so the RV empties later and P2 comes after A2.
A loud, sometimes palpable P2 means high pulmonary artery pressure snapping the valve shut.
A dysplastic, stenotic pulmonary valve is the commonest heart lesion in Noonan syndrome.

resident.text: After Fallot repair, follow RV size and function with CMR and replace the pulmonary valve before the RV fails or VT appears.
Typical dome-shaped congenital valvar pulmonary stenosis is treated with balloon valvuloplasty.

saq.q: Explain why S2 splits on inspiration.
saq.a: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, so RV ejection lasts longer and P2 comes later than A2.

saq.q: An adult whose tetralogy of Fallot was repaired in childhood now tires easily. What valve problem do you expect and how do you follow it?
saq.a: Severe pulmonary regurgitation with RV dilation. Follow RV volumes and function with CMR and refer for pulmonary valve replacement before RV failure or VT.

sources: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guideline
ACC/AHA 2018 adult congenital heart disease guideline
verify: Noonan: pulmonary stenosis the commonest lesion

cards.name: Papillary muscles (LV)
cards.core: Two muscle columns in the LV that anchor the mitral chordae and stop the leaflets flipping into the LA.

quick.text: Rise from the LV wall: **anterolateral** and **posteromedial**
Contract in systole to keep the chordae taut, so the **mitral leaflets don't prolapse**
**ALPM**: LAD + LCx · **PMPM**: usually the PDA alone
**PMPM rupture** after inferior MI → acute severe MR, shock

parts.name: Anterolateral
parts.note: Larger, with two arteries (LAD diagonals and LCx marginals), so it rarely ruptures.

parts.name: Posteromedial
parts.note: Usually one artery (the PDA), so it is the one that ruptures after inferior MI.

anatomy.summary: Two muscle columns from the LV wall; chordae from each go to both mitral leaflets.
anatomy.detail: The anterolateral muscle arises from the anterolateral wall, the posteromedial from the inferior wall near the septum. Each holds the matching half of both leaflets. The RV has its own (anterior, posterior, septal) for the tricuspid valve.

function.summary: They contract with the ventricle so the chordae stay tight as the LV shortens.
function.detail: Without that tension the leaflet edges would be pushed into the LA in systole. When the LV dilates they move apart and tether the leaflets (secondary MR).

supply.summary: ALPM has two arteries; the PMPM usually one.
supply.detail: ALPM: LAD diagonals and LCx obtuse marginals. PMPM: the PDA (from the RCA in right-dominant hearts, the LCx in left-dominant).

relations.why: Rupture or dysfunction causes MR.
The PMPM sits on it, so inferior MI threatens it.

echo.text: Both muscles at mid-ventricle, at about 4 and 8 o'clock.
The anterolateral muscle along the lateral wall.

cut.text: Both muscles and their chordae.
Two bumps on the inner LV wall.

complications.name: Papillary muscle rupture
complications.mechanism: Infarction of the single-supply PMPM tears the muscle or one of its heads, freeing its chordae.
complications.presentation: Usually days 2–7 after MI: sudden pulmonary oedema and shock; the murmur may be soft.
complications.hook: Sudden oedema and shock days after MI

complications.name: Papillary muscle dysfunction
complications.mechanism: Ischaemia without rupture weakens the muscle, so the leaflets don't close fully.
complications.presentation: MR that comes and goes with angina.
complications.hook: MR that comes and goes with ischaemia

complications.name: Tethering (secondary) MR
complications.mechanism: A dilated LV pulls the muscles apart and the leaflets with them.
complications.presentation: MR with normal leaflets in heart failure.

complications.name: Abnormal papillary muscles in HCM
complications.mechanism: Displaced or extra papillary muscles push the mitral apparatus towards the LVOT.
complications.presentation: Adds to outflow obstruction.
complications.hook: Adds to outflow obstruction in HCM

student.text: It usually has one artery (the PDA); the ALPM has two, so one blocked artery rarely kills it.
Mechanical complications (papillary rupture, septal rupture, free-wall rupture) cluster in the first week, mostly days 2–7.

resident.text: Urgent echo. Papillary rupture needs emergency surgery, with support meanwhile (vasodilator if BP allows, IABP or mechanical support).

resident.hook: A soft murmur doesn't rule it out
resident.text: In acute severe MR the LA and LV pressures equalise quickly, so the murmur may be short or absent.

saq.q: Why is the posteromedial papillary muscle more likely to rupture after MI than the anterolateral one?
saq.a: It usually has one artery (the PDA); the anterolateral has two (LAD and LCx), so a single occlusion rarely infarcts it completely.

saq.q: Three days after an inferior STEMI: sudden pulmonary oedema and hypotension. What do you look for, and with what test?
saq.a: Mechanical complications: papillary muscle rupture (acute MR), ventricular septal rupture, or free-wall rupture with tamponade. Urgent bedside echo.

verify: PMPM single supply in most hearts

cards.name: Chordae tendineae
cards.core: Fine fibrous cords from the papillary muscles to the leaflets: the valve's guy-ropes.

quick.text: Run from the **papillary muscles** to the **mitral and tricuspid** leaflets
Stop the leaflets **flipping into the atrium** in systole
A **torn chord** → flail leaflet → acute severe MR
Flail: the leaflet tip points **into the LA** in systole

anatomy.summary: Thin collagen cords: primary to the free edge, secondary to the underside, tertiary from the wall to the posterior leaflet base.
anatomy.detail: Each LV papillary muscle sends chordae to both mitral leaflets. Primary (marginal) chordae hold the edge; secondary chordae attach to the underside and help keep the LV's shape; tertiary chordae run from the wall to the base of the posterior leaflet. The tricuspid also takes chordae straight from the septum.

function.summary: Hold the leaflets in a sealed position against systolic pressure.
function.detail: Secondary chordae also tie the valve to the LV and help its shape and function, which is why surgeons try to keep them.

supply.summary: No vessels: nourished from the blood around them.
supply.detail: Avascular collagen.

relations.why: Their anchors.
A torn chord to P2 is the commonest cause of a flail mitral leaflet.

echo.text: Chordae under the leaflets; a flail tip in systole.
The subvalvular apparatus of both AV valves.

cut.text: Mitral chordae to both papillary muscles.
Tricuspid chordae, some from the septum.

complications.name: Chordal rupture with flail leaflet
complications.mechanism: Myxomatous degeneration, endocarditis or trauma tears a chord; the free edge flails into the LA.
complications.presentation: Sudden breathlessness; severe eccentric MR (often P2).

complications.name: Rheumatic chordal fusion
complications.mechanism: Chordae thicken, shorten and fuse.
complications.presentation: Adds below-valve narrowing in rheumatic MS and makes balloon valvotomy less successful.
complications.hook: Thick, short chordae in rheumatic MS

student.text: Prolapse: the leaflet body bulges into the LA but the tip still points to the LV. Flail: a torn chord lets the tip point into the LA.
Thick, fused chordae lower the chance that balloon valvotomy works (part of the Wilkins score).

resident.text: A flail segment almost always means severe MR; an isolated P2 flail is very repairable.
Flail and prolapse jets hug the LA wall, so colour area underestimates them: use vena contracta, PISA and pulmonary vein flow.

saq.q: What is the difference between a prolapsing and a flail mitral leaflet?
saq.a: In prolapse the leaflet body bulges into the LA but its tip still points to the LV. In a flail leaflet a torn chord lets the tip itself point into the LA.
keys: Prolapse: body bulges, tip to LV

saq.q: A P2 flail with an eccentric jet: why may colour Doppler underestimate it, and what do you measure instead?
saq.a: Eccentric jets hug the LA wall and lose area (Coanda effect). Use vena contracta, PISA (EROA, regurgitant volume) and pulmonary vein flow reversal.

cards.name: Moderator band
cards.core: A muscular bridge across the RV from the septum to the anterior papillary muscle, carrying the right bundle branch.

quick.text: Crosses the **RV** from the septum to the **anterior papillary muscle**
Carries the **right bundle branch** so the anterior papillary muscle contracts on time
A band near the RV apex that **identifies the RV** on echo
Easily mistaken for an **RV clot or mass**

anatomy.summary: Part of the septomarginal trabecula, spanning the lower RV cavity from the septum to the anterior papillary muscle.
anatomy.detail: It crosses the apical third of the RV. The right bundle branch travels inside it, and its artery usually comes from the first septal branch of the LAD.

function.summary: A shortcut for the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle.
function.detail: Early activation of the anterior papillary muscle tightens the tricuspid chordae before RV pressure rises. The old idea that it stops the RV over-stretching gave it the name 'moderator'.

supply.summary: Usually the first septal perforator of the LAD (the moderator-band artery).
supply.detail: This artery can link LAD and RCA territories as a collateral.

relations.why: Injury here can cause RBBB; some PVCs and rare VF triggers start in its Purkinje fibres.
Its far anchor.

echo.text: A band across the RV near the apex.
The same band, closer to the probe.

cut.text: The bridge from the septum to the anterior papillary muscle.

ecg.text: Moderator-band PVCs: LBBB-like QRS with a superior axis and a late precordial transition.

complications.name: Moderator-band PVCs and VF
complications.mechanism: Purkinje fibres in the band fire ectopic beats that can trigger VF.
complications.presentation: LBBB-like PVCs with a superior axis; rarely idiopathic VF.
complications.hook: LBBB-like PVCs; a rare VF trigger

complications.name: Mistaken for a mass
complications.mechanism: A thick band is read as RV thrombus or tumour.
complications.presentation: Imaging pitfall; avoid needless anticoagulation or work-up.
complications.hook: A normal band read as a mass

student.text: Moderator band, coarse trabeculae and a lower tricuspid hinge mark the RV, whichever side it lies on.
The right bundle branch takes the band as a shortcut to the anterior papillary muscle.

resident.text: A straight band joining the lower septum to the anterior papillary muscle is the moderator band.
Moderator-band PVCs have a superior axis; RVOT PVCs have an inferior axis. Both look LBBB-like.

saq.q: Name two features that identify the RV on echo, one of them a structure carrying the conduction system.
saq.a: The moderator band (carrying the right bundle branch) and a tricuspid hinge closer to the apex; coarse trabeculae also help.

saq.q: A PVC has an LBBB-like shape. How does the axis help separate an RVOT origin from a moderator-band origin?
saq.a: Inferior axis = starts high (RVOT); superior axis = starts low in the RV (moderator band or apex).

verify: Moderator-band PVC morphology (superior axis, late transition)
Artery from the first septal perforator

cards.name: Central fibrous body
cards.core: The strongest part of the heart's fibrous skeleton, joining the mitral, tricuspid and aortic rings; the His bundle pierces it.

quick.text: At the centre of the heart, where the **mitral, tricuspid and aortic** rings meet
**Insulates** the atria from the ventricles
The **His bundle** is the only normal path through it
Valve surgery, TAVI or a root abscess here → **heart block**

anatomy.summary: The right fibrous trigone plus the membranous septum: the centre of the fibrous skeleton.
anatomy.detail: The fibrous skeleton is the four valve rings joined by the right and left fibrous trigones. The right trigone and the membranous septum form the central fibrous body, between the mitral, tricuspid and aortic rings. The AV node rests on its right-atrial side, and the His bundle passes through it to the crest of the ventricular septum.

function.summary: Anchors the valves and electrically separates atria from ventricles.
function.detail: Fibrous tissue does not conduct, so every normal impulse has to pass through the AV node and His bundle. An accessory pathway is a muscle bridge that crosses the rings somewhere else.

supply.summary: Fibrous tissue with few vessels; the His bundle inside it is fed by the AV nodal artery and LAD septal branches.
supply.detail: That dual supply of the His bundle is why it often survives an inferior MI that blocks the AV node.

relations.why: Passes through it.
Disease or surgery at any of them can injure the conduction axis.
Cross the rings elsewhere: WPW.

echo.text: At the crux, where the valve hinges meet the septum.

cut.text: Between the valve rings at the centre of the base.
Where the AV valve hinges meet the septum.

ecg.text: Damage here: PR prolongation, bundle branch block or complete heart block.

complications.name: Heart block after valve surgery or TAVI
complications.mechanism: Oedema, sutures or the prosthesis press on the His bundle where it passes through.
complications.presentation: New LBBB or complete heart block after the procedure.
complications.hook: New block after aortic or mitral procedures

complications.name: Root abscess spreading here
complications.mechanism: Aortic valve endocarditis burrows into the fibrous body.
complications.presentation: New PR prolongation or heart block in endocarditis.

complications.name: Age-related fibrosis and calcification (Lev disease)
complications.mechanism: The skeleton calcifies and damages the conduction axis passing through it.
complications.presentation: Slowly progressive conduction block in older people.

student.hook: Why WPW needs an extra pathway
student.text: The fibrous rings block conduction; only the His bundle crosses. An accessory pathway is a muscle bridge that escapes this insulation.
Mitral, tricuspid and aortic valves all meet here, which is why surgery on any of them can cause heart block.

resident.text: A new long PR or AV block in aortic valve endocarditis suggests spread into this region: urgent TOE and surgical review.
Fibrosis of the skeleton (Lev) or of the conduction system itself (Lenègre) is a common cause of progressive block.

saq.q: Why is the His bundle the only normal electrical route from atria to ventricles?
saq.a: The fibrous skeleton (valve rings and central fibrous body) does not conduct; the His bundle is the only muscle path that pierces it.
keys: His pierces the central fibrous body

saq.q: Aortic valve endocarditis; the PR is now 280 ms. What does this suggest and what next?
saq.a: Spread of infection into the root and central fibrous body (abscess) next to the conduction axis. Urgent TOE and early surgical review.

sources: ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 bradycardia and conduction delay guideline
verify: His bundle dual supply (AV nodal artery + LAD septal)

cards.name: Left main coronary artery (LM)
cards.core: A short trunk that carries the blood for most of the left ventricle before it splits into the LAD and LCx, so one lesion here threatens almost the whole LV.

quick.text: Leaves the **left aortic sinus**, runs between the **pulmonary trunk and the LAA**
Splits into **LAD + LCx** (± ramus): most of the LV in a right-dominant heart
**ST↑ in aVR** + diffuse ST↓ (≥ 6 leads) = global subendocardial ischaemia
Acute occlusion → **cardiogenic shock** or sudden death
Significant LM disease → **revascularise** (CABG; PCI if anatomy simple)

anatomy.summary: A short trunk from the left aortic sinus that passes behind the pulmonary trunk and splits under the LAA.
anatomy.detail: Arises from the left coronary (left aortic) sinus, just above the left coronary cusp. It runs to the left between the pulmonary trunk (in front) and the left atrial appendage (to the left) and divides in the left AV groove into the LAD and the LCx. In some hearts a third branch, the ramus intermedius, leaves between them (trifurcation) and runs over the lateral wall like a diagonal or obtuse marginal.

function.summary: A single inflow for the left coronary system: all LAD and LCx flow passes through it.
function.detail: Everything the LAD and LCx supply depends on this one segment. A stenosis here reduces flow to both territories at once, so ischaemia is global rather than regional. As in all LV arteries, flow happens mostly in diastole.

supply.summary: Territory: LAD + LCx territories together (anterior, septal, lateral, and posterior if left-dominant).
supply.detail: Territory: the anterior wall, the anterior two thirds of the septum, the apex and the lateral wall; also the posterior wall and inferior septum in a left-dominant heart. Venous return: great cardiac vein and coronary sinus.

relations.why: The LM runs just behind it; an anomalous left coronary can be squeezed between the aorta and pulmonary trunk on exercise.
The LM and proximal LCx lie under the LAA: a landmark for surgeons and for LAA occlusion devices.
Its ostium sits above this cusp, so a bulky calcified cusp or a TAVI valve can block it.

echo.text: Ostium of the LM at about 4 o'clock on the aortic root (a good image is not always possible in adults).

cut.text: Left coronary ostium above the left coronary cusp (turn coronaries on).

ecg.text: ST elevation in aVR (± V1) with ST depression in six or more leads: suggests LM or three-vessel disease, not specific.

complications.name: Left main occlusion or critical stenosis
complications.mechanism: Flow to both the LAD and LCx territories falls at once, so most of the LV becomes ischaemic.
complications.presentation: Chest pain with hypotension or shock; ST elevation in aVR with widespread ST depression; often pulmonary oedema or cardiac arrest.

complications.name: Coronary obstruction during TAVI
complications.mechanism: The new valve pushes the native left cusp against a low LM ostium or a narrow sinus.
complications.presentation: Sudden hypotension and ST changes as the valve is deployed.
complications.hook: Shock as the TAVI valve opens

complications.name: Anomalous left coronary from the right sinus
complications.mechanism: The LM arises from the wrong sinus and runs between the aorta and pulmonary trunk, which can compress it during exercise.
complications.presentation: Exertional syncope or chest pain, or sudden death in a young athlete; resting ECG often normal.
complications.hook: Exertional syncope or sudden death, young

student.text: ST elevation in aVR with ST depression everywhere else means the inner layer of most of the LV is ischaemic, as in LM or three-vessel disease.
An LM lesion is treated as two-vessel disease at minimum, because both the LAD and LCx sit beyond it.
The LM feeds most of the LV muscle, so an acute occlusion leaves too little working muscle to keep blood pressure up.

resident.text: Significant LM disease improves with revascularisation. CABG is the default; PCI is a reasonable alternative when the rest of the anatomy is simple (low SYNTAX score).
Ostial LM disease can damp or 'ventricularise' the catheter pressure on engagement: withdraw and reassess before injecting.

resident.hook: Not every aVR elevation is LM
resident.text: The same pattern appears with three-vessel disease, severe aortic stenosis, or demand ischaemia from tachycardia or anaemia.

fellow.text: Intravascular imaging guides LM assessment and stent sizing; angiography often misjudges ostial and distal LM lesions.

saq.q: ST elevation in aVR with ST depression in I, II and V4–V6. What does it suggest, and why?
saq.a: Diffuse subendocardial ischaemia, as in left main or three-vessel disease. The ischaemic inner layer of most of the LV makes the ST vector point away from the apex and towards aVR.

saq.q: Why does a left main occlusion often present in shock?
saq.a: The LM carries the flow for both the LAD and LCx, so most of the LV becomes ischaemic at once and cannot keep cardiac output up.

saq.q: A 70-year-old with stable angina has a 70 % distal LM stenosis and diabetes with multivessel disease. Preferred revascularisation?
saq.a: CABG: significant LM disease with diabetes and complex multivessel anatomy has the best long-term outcome with surgery (LIMA to LAD). PCI is reserved for simple anatomy or high surgical risk.
keys: PCI if simple anatomy / high risk

sources: Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy (coronary arteries)
verify: 'Most of the LV' wording for the LM territory in right dominance
Ramus intermedius frequency (not stated on the card)

cards.name: Diagonal branches (D1, D2)

parts.name: First diagonal (D1)
parts.note: The largest diagonal; it feeds the high lateral wall. Its occlusion is the classic high lateral MI (I, aVL).

parts.name: Second diagonal (D2)
parts.note: Further down the LAD; supplies the mid anterolateral wall.

cards.core: Branches of the LAD that run diagonally over the anterolateral LV wall; a D1 occlusion causes a small but easily missed high lateral MI.

quick.text: Leave the **LAD** and run **diagonally** over the anterolateral wall
Anterolateral wall + share of the **anterolateral papillary muscle**
D1 occlusion → ST↑ **I, aVL** (± V2) with **reciprocal ST↓ in III**
LAD–D1 **bifurcation** lesions are harder to stent

anatomy.summary: Branches from the LAD that run diagonally over the anterolateral LV wall towards the obtuse margin.
anatomy.detail: Two or three diagonals usually leave the LAD on its left side and run over the anterolateral wall. D1 is the first and often the largest. They run on the epicardial surface, opposite in direction to the septal perforators, which dive into the septum.

function.summary: Supply the anterolateral LV wall and help feed the anterolateral papillary muscle.
function.detail: They extend the LAD territory sideways. Together with the obtuse marginals of the LCx they supply the anterolateral papillary muscle, which therefore has two sources.

supply.summary: Territory: high lateral and anterolateral LV walls.
supply.detail: Territory: the anterolateral (high lateral) LV wall and part of the anterolateral papillary muscle. Venous return: tributaries of the great cardiac vein.

relations.why: A dual supply (diagonals + obtuse marginals) is why this muscle rarely ruptures after MI.
Share the lateral wall with the LCx; their territories meet and vary between people.

echo.text: Anterolateral segments at mid-ventricle.
Lateral wall (shared with the LCx).

cut.text: Anterolateral LV wall and the anterolateral papillary muscle.

ecg.text: I and aVL (high lateral); sometimes V2, with ST depression in III and aVF.

complications.name: High lateral STEMI (D1 occlusion)
complications.mechanism: Occlusion of D1 infarcts the high lateral wall, which only I and aVL face directly.
complications.presentation: ST elevation in I and aVL, often subtle, with clear reciprocal ST depression in III; sometimes ST elevation in V2 as well.
complications.hook: Subtle ST↑ I, aVL; clear ST↓ in III

complications.name: Side-branch closure during LAD stenting
complications.mechanism: A stent across the LAD shifts plaque or the carina into the D1 ostium (plaque shift).
complications.presentation: Chest pain and lateral ST change during or after PCI; a small troponin rise.

student.text: Diagonals run over the surface of the anterolateral wall; septals dive into the septum. Both come from the LAD.
In a small high lateral MI, the ST depression in III is often easier to see than the ST elevation in aVL.

resident.text: ST↑ in I, aVL and V2 with ST↓ in III is a D1 (or proximal LAD) occlusion, a STEMI that is easily missed.
LAD–D1 lesions are classified by which limbs are diseased (Medina). Usually stent the main branch and only treat the side branch if needed (provisional strategy).
Its double supply (diagonals + OMs) makes rupture rare; the posteromedial muscle with one supply is the one that tears.

saq.q: ST elevation in I and aVL with ST depression in III. Which wall and which artery?
saq.a: The high lateral wall: usually the first diagonal (or a proximal LAD / OM). III shows the mirror image.

saq.q: Why is papillary muscle rupture after MI almost always the posteromedial muscle?
saq.a: The anterolateral muscle has two supplies (LAD diagonals and LCx marginals); the posteromedial muscle usually has one (the PDA), so a single occlusion can infarct it completely.

verify: 'South African flag' sign description (ST↑ I, aVL, V2; ST↓ III)

cards.name: Left circumflex artery (LCx)

parts.name: Proximal LCx
parts.note: Under the LAA, from the left main to the first obtuse marginal.

parts.name: Distal LCx
parts.note: Along the left AV groove towards the crux; gives the PDA in a left-dominant heart (about 1 in 10).

cards.core: The artery in the left AV groove that feeds the lateral and posterior LV walls; its infarcts are the most often 'ECG-silent'.

quick.text: Runs in the **left AV groove** beside the mitral annulus, under the LAA
**Lateral** and **posterior** LV walls via the obtuse marginals
Often **silent** on the 12-lead; posterior MI = **ST↓ V1–V3 with tall R** → record V7–V9
Close to the **mitral annulus**: can be injured in mitral surgery
**Left-dominant**: the LCx gives the PDA and the AV nodal artery

anatomy.summary: From the left main, round the left AV groove under the LAA towards the back of the heart.
anatomy.detail: Arises from the left main and curves to the left and back in the left AV groove, under the left atrial appendage and next to the mitral annulus. The great cardiac vein (becoming the coronary sinus) runs with it. Branches: obtuse marginals over the lateral wall, atrial branches, and in about 40 % the SA nodal artery. In a left-dominant heart it reaches the crux and gives the PDA and the AV nodal artery.

function.summary: Supplies the lateral and posterior LV walls, part of the LA, and sometimes the SA or AV node.
function.detail: Its territory faces left and backwards, away from most precordial electrodes. That geometry, not its size, explains why LCx occlusions are so often missed on the standard ECG.

supply.summary: Territory: lateral and posterolateral LV wall (+ inferior wall and septum if left-dominant).
supply.detail: Territory: the lateral and posterolateral LV wall, part of the anterolateral papillary muscle, the LA; in left dominance also the inferior wall, inferior septum and posteromedial papillary muscle. Venous return: great cardiac vein and coronary sinus.

relations.why: Lies a few millimetres away: mitral repair or replacement sutures and coronary-sinus annuloplasty devices can kink or compress it.
Runs alongside in the same groove; the vein crosses over the artery.
The proximal LCx lies under the LAA ostium (watch during LAA occlusion).

echo.text: Lateral wall (anterolateral segments).
Inferolateral and anterolateral segments.
Inferolateral (posterior) wall: the lower wall in this view.

cut.text: Left AV groove next to the mitral annulus (turn coronaries on).
Lateral and inferolateral LV wall.

ecg.text: Lateral leads I, aVL, V5–V6; posterior wall seen only as a mirror image in V1–V3 (ST↓, tall R) or directly in V7–V9.

complications.name: Lateral STEMI
complications.mechanism: Occlusion of the LCx or an obtuse marginal infarcts the lateral wall.
complications.presentation: ST elevation in I, aVL, V5–V6, often small.
complications.hook: ST↑ I, aVL, V5–V6, often small

complications.name: Posterior MI
complications.mechanism: Occlusion of the distal LCx (or a large OM) infarcts the posterior (inferolateral) wall, which no standard lead faces.
complications.presentation: ST depression with upright T and a tall R in V1–V3; ST elevation in V7–V9 confirms a STEMI equivalent.
complications.hook: ST↓ V1–V3 + tall R → do V7–V9

complications.name: Missed occlusion MI
complications.mechanism: A complete LCx occlusion produces no ST elevation in the standard leads.
complications.presentation: Ongoing chest pain, rising troponin, 'non-diagnostic' ECG; regional wall-motion loss on echo.

complications.name: LCx injury in mitral surgery
complications.mechanism: Annular sutures or a ring placed close to the artery kink or occlude it.
complications.presentation: New lateral ischaemia or arrhythmia after mitral repair or replacement.

student.text: Its territory faces left and back, away from V1–V6, so a full occlusion can look normal on the 12-lead.
Flip the ECG over: ST depression and tall R in V1–V2 are the mirror image of a posterior MI. Record V7–V9.
The artery that gives the PDA is the dominant one: RCA in most people, LCx in about 1 in 10.

resident.hook: Pain + normal ECG = still think OMI
resident.text: Persistent ischaemic pain despite medical therapy needs urgent angiography (within 2 h) even without ST elevation; many of these are LCx occlusions.
Can cause inferior + posterior + lateral MI and AV block, because it then feeds the PDA and AV nodal artery.
An echo showing new lateral or inferolateral hypokinesis in ongoing pain supports an occlusion the ECG cannot show.

fellow.text: Percutaneous mitral annuloplasty through the coronary sinus can compress the LCx where the vein crosses over it; check the anatomy on CT first.

saq.q: Chest pain; ST depression with a tall R wave in V1–V3. What is the likely diagnosis, and what extra leads will you record?
saq.a: Posterior MI, usually from the LCx (or RCA). Record V7–V9: ST elevation there confirms it.

saq.q: Why is the LCx called 'electrically silent'?
saq.a: Its territory (lateral and posterior wall) faces left and back, away from the standard precordial leads, so an occlusion may show little or no ST elevation.

saq.q: Ongoing ischaemic pain for 40 minutes, nondiagnostic ECG, new inferolateral hypokinesis on echo. Management?
saq.a: Treat as a possible occlusion MI (often LCx): immediate invasive strategy (angiography within 2 hours) for refractory pain, plus standard antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy.

sources: Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy (coronary arteries)
verify: LCx gives the SA nodal artery in ≈ 40 %

cards.name: Obtuse marginal branches (OM1, OM2)

parts.name: First obtuse marginal (OM1)
parts.note: Usually the largest LCx branch; often a bigger artery than the LCx beyond it.

parts.name: Second obtuse marginal (OM2)
parts.note: Further along the LCx; supplies the posterolateral wall.

cards.core: Branches of the LCx that run down the rounded (obtuse) left margin of the heart and feed the lateral LV wall.

quick.text: Run down the **obtuse (left) margin** of the heart from the LCx
**Lateral** LV wall + share of the **anterolateral papillary muscle**
Occlusion → **lateral STEMI**: ST↑ I, aVL, V5–V6 (often small)
A large OM is often the **culprit in 'NSTEMI'** that is really an occlusion

anatomy.summary: Branches of the LCx that run down the left (obtuse) margin of the heart towards the apex.
anatomy.detail: The heart's left border is rounded, the 'obtuse' margin, as opposed to the sharp 'acute' right margin. The obtuse marginals leave the LCx in the AV groove and run down this border. Their number and size vary, and they share the lateral wall with the diagonals.

function.summary: The main supply to the lateral LV wall.
function.detail: They carry most of the LCx flow to the lateral wall and help supply the anterolateral papillary muscle.

supply.summary: Territory: lateral and posterolateral LV wall.
supply.detail: Territory: the lateral and posterolateral LV wall and part of the anterolateral papillary muscle. Venous return: the left marginal vein into the great cardiac vein.

relations.why: Share the lateral wall, so the culprit for a lateral MI can be either.
Runs with them; one of the preferred veins for a CRT LV lead (lateral wall).

echo.text: Lateral wall.
Anterolateral and inferolateral segments.

cut.text: Lateral LV wall.

ecg.text: I, aVL, V5–V6.

complications.name: Lateral STEMI
complications.mechanism: Occlusion of an OM infarcts the lateral wall.
complications.presentation: Small ST elevation in I, aVL, V5–V6 with reciprocal ST depression inferiorly; easily labelled NSTEMI.

complications.name: Ischaemic mitral regurgitation
complications.mechanism: Lateral and inferolateral scar pulls the papillary muscles outwards and tethers the posterior leaflet.
complications.presentation: A new or worsening MR murmur after a lateral or inferolateral MI; heart failure.

student.text: The left border of the heart is rounded (obtuse): LCx marginals. The right border is sharp (acute): the RCA's acute marginal.
Only I, aVL, V5 and V6 look at the lateral wall, so lateral infarcts often show only small ST changes.

resident.text: In NSTEMI with a total occlusion at angiography, the culprit is most often the LCx or an OM.
CRT works best when the LV lead sits over the lateral wall, which is why the lateral marginal vein is the target.

saq.q: What does 'obtuse marginal' mean, and which wall does an OM supply?
saq.a: The left border of the heart is rounded (obtuse); the OMs run down it from the LCx and supply the lateral LV wall.

saq.q: Why can a lateral wall infarct be mislabelled as NSTEMI?
saq.a: Few leads face the lateral wall (I, aVL, V5–V6) and the ST elevation is often small or below the criteria, so a total occlusion may not meet STEMI criteria.

verify: OM1 often larger than the LCx beyond it (wording)

cards.name: Right coronary artery (RCA)

parts.name: Conus branch
parts.note: The first branch, to the RV outflow tract; a common collateral to the LAD (circle of Vieussens). Has its own ostium in some people.

parts.name: RV branch
parts.note: Feed the RV free wall; a proximal RCA occlusion above them causes RV infarction.

parts.name: RV branch
parts.note: Feed the RV free wall; a proximal RCA occlusion above them causes RV infarction.

parts.name: Acute marginal
parts.note: Runs along the sharp (acute) lower right border of the heart to the RV free wall.

parts.name: Right posterolateral branch
parts.note: Beyond the crux in a right-dominant heart; supplies the inferolateral LV wall.

cards.core: The artery of the right AV groove: it feeds the RV, the inferior LV wall in most people, and usually both the SA and AV nodes, so its occlusions cause infarcts with rhythm problems.

quick.text: From the **right aortic sinus** round the **right AV groove** to the **crux**
**RV**, **inferior LV** (via PDA), **SA node** (≈ 60 %), **AV node** (≈ 85 %)
Inferior STEMI: ST↑ **III > II**, ST↓ in I and aVL
**Proximal** occlusion takes the RV branches → **RV infarct**: no nitrates
Inferior MI + **bradycardia/AV block** = nodal ischaemia + vagal reflex

anatomy.summary: From the right aortic sinus, between the pulmonary trunk and the RA appendage, down the right AV groove to the crux.
anatomy.detail: Arises from the right coronary (right aortic) sinus and runs forwards and right between the pulmonary trunk and the RA appendage into the right AV groove, beside the tricuspid annulus. Proximal: conus branch, SA nodal artery (about 60 %) and RV branches. Mid: the acute marginal along the sharp lower right border. Distal: at the crux, in a right-dominant heart, it makes a U-turn, gives the AV nodal artery, the PDA and the posterolateral branches.

function.summary: Supplies the RV, the inferior LV and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes.
function.detail: Because the RV runs at low pressure, RV branches get flow in systole and diastole. The nodal branches explain why RCA infarcts so often cause sinus bradycardia and AV block.

supply.summary: Territory: RV, inferior LV wall and inferior septum (if right-dominant), SA and AV nodes.
supply.detail: Territory: the RV free wall, the inferior LV wall, the inferior third of the septum and the posteromedial papillary muscle (via the PDA), the SA node (about 60 %), the AV node (about 80–90 %). Venous return: small cardiac vein and anterior cardiac veins (straight into the RA).

relations.why: The RCA lies right next to it in the AV groove: tricuspid surgery and some ablation lines (CTI) pass close to it.
Its ostium sits above this cusp; the right cusp is the anterior one.
Runs with it in the right AV groove.

echo.text: Origin of the RCA at about 10–11 o'clock on the aortic root.
RV free wall (TAPSE) and inferoseptum.
Inferior and inferoseptal segments, RV free wall.

cut.text: Right AV groove beside the tricuspid annulus (turn coronaries on).
Inferior LV wall and RV free wall.

ecg.text: II, III, aVF (III > II suggests RCA); V4R for RV involvement; V1 ST elevation in RV infarction.

complications.name: Inferior STEMI
complications.mechanism: Occlusion of the mid or distal RCA infarcts the inferior LV wall (via the PDA).
complications.presentation: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with III > II and reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL.
complications.hook: ST↑ III > II, ST↓ in aVL

complications.name: RV infarction
complications.mechanism: Proximal occlusion, above the RV branches, stops the RV free wall from pumping; the LV loses its preload.
complications.presentation: Inferior STEMI with hypotension, raised JVP and clear lungs; ST elevation in V4R; collapse after nitrates.

complications.name: Sinus bradycardia and AV block
complications.mechanism: Ischaemia of the SA or AV nodal artery plus the vagal Bezold–Jarisch reflex from the inferior wall.
complications.presentation: Sinus bradycardia, first-degree block, Wenckebach or complete block with a narrow escape; usually transient.

complications.name: Posteromedial papillary muscle rupture
complications.mechanism: The PDA is usually its only supply; infarction makes it tear, typically 2–7 days after MI.
complications.presentation: Sudden pulmonary oedema and shock with a new (sometimes soft) murmur of severe MR.

student.text: The RCA's inferior territory points more to the right, towards III. In an LCx inferior MI, II ≥ III and I/aVL are often isoelectric or up.
In every inferior STEMI record V4R: ST elevation of 1 mm or more means the RV is involved.
The RCA usually feeds both nodes, and the inferior wall triggers a vagal reflex, so bradycardia and AV block are common and often respond to atropine.

resident.text: Preload-dependent: stop nitrates and diuretics, give careful fluid, keep AV synchrony, reperfuse quickly.
Usually a narrow escape at 40–60 bpm that resolves within days after reperfusion; permanent pacing is rarely needed.
The conus branch often supplies collaterals to an occluded LAD, which can protect the anterior wall.

fellow.text: When the conus branch has its own ostium, a 'missing' RVOT supply on the RCA angiogram is not an occlusion: inject the right sinus separately.

saq.q: Inferior STEMI with ST elevation in III greater than II and ST depression in aVL. Which artery, and which extra lead must you record?
saq.a: The RCA. Record V4R to look for RV involvement (proximal occlusion).

saq.q: Why does an inferior MI often cause bradycardia?
saq.a: The RCA usually supplies the SA and AV nodes, and inferior wall ischaemia triggers a vagal reflex (Bezold–Jarisch).

saq.q: Inferior STEMI with complete heart block, narrow escape at 50 bpm, BP 100/60. What level is the block, and what is the likely course?
saq.a: AV nodal block from AV nodal artery ischaemia and vagal tone; the escape is junctional. It usually resolves within days after reperfusion; atropine or temporary pacing if unstable, permanent pacing rarely needed.

cards.name: Posterior descending artery (PDA)
cards.core: The artery in the inferior interventricular groove: it feeds the inferior wall, the inferior septum and the posteromedial papillary muscle, and its origin defines coronary dominance.

quick.text: Runs in the **inferior interventricular groove** from the crux towards the apex
The artery that gives the PDA is **dominant**: RCA in most, LCx ≈ 10 %
**Inferior wall**, **inferior septum** and the **posteromedial papillary muscle**
Single supply → **papillary muscle rupture** → acute severe MR

anatomy.summary: From the crux (usually the RCA) down the inferior interventricular groove beside the middle cardiac vein.
anatomy.detail: At the crux, where the AV and interventricular grooves meet on the inferior surface, the dominant artery turns and runs down the inferior (posterior) interventricular groove towards the apex. The middle cardiac vein runs beside it. It gives inferior septal perforators to the lower part of the septum.

function.summary: Supplies the inferior wall, the inferior third of the septum and the posteromedial papillary muscle.
function.detail: Its septal branches meet those of the LAD inside the septum, a common collateral route when one of them is blocked.

supply.summary: Territory: inferior LV wall, inferior septum, posteromedial papillary muscle.
supply.detail: Territory: the inferior (diaphragmatic) LV wall, the inferior third of the septum and the posteromedial papillary muscle. Venous return: the middle cardiac vein into the coronary sinus.

relations.why: Runs with it in the same groove.
Usually its only supply, so a PDA infarct can rupture it.
An inferior MI can rupture the basal inferior septum (VSR), which has a worse prognosis than an apical one.

echo.text: Inferior and inferoseptal segments; posteromedial papillary muscle.
Inferoseptum (the septum in this view).

cut.text: Inferior wall and the posteromedial papillary muscle.

ecg.text: II, III, aVF.

complications.name: Inferior STEMI
complications.mechanism: Occlusion of the PDA or the artery that feeds it infarcts the inferior wall.
complications.presentation: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal changes in I and aVL.

complications.name: Posteromedial papillary muscle rupture
complications.mechanism: The muscle depends on one artery; infarction weakens it until it tears.
complications.presentation: Days 2–7 after an inferior MI: sudden breathlessness, pulmonary oedema, shock; a flail mitral leaflet on echo. The murmur can be soft or absent.
complications.hook: Day 2–7: flash oedema, soft or no murmur

complications.name: Inferior ventricular septal rupture
complications.mechanism: Necrosis of the basal inferior septum tears.
complications.presentation: New harsh holosystolic murmur, shock, step-up in O₂ saturation in the RV; worse prognosis than anterior VSR.
complications.hook: New harsh murmur + shock after inferior MI

student.text: 'Right-dominant' does not mean the RCA is bigger: it means the RCA gives the PDA.
It has one artery (the PDA); the anterolateral muscle has two (LAD + LCx).

resident.text: In acute papillary muscle rupture the LA is small and stiff, so pressures equalise fast and the murmur can be short or silent. Echo urgently in post-MI pulmonary oedema.
If the LCx gives the PDA, an LCx occlusion can cause inferior, posterior and lateral MI together.

saq.q: What defines coronary dominance?
saq.a: The artery that gives the posterior descending artery (PDA): the RCA in most people, the LCx in about 1 in 10, both in a co-dominant heart.

saq.q: Why is the posteromedial papillary muscle more likely to rupture than the anterolateral one?
saq.a: It is usually supplied only by the PDA, so a single occlusion can infarct it; the anterolateral muscle has a dual supply.

saq.q: Day 4 after inferior MI: sudden pulmonary oedema and hypotension, no loud murmur. Most important test and likely diagnosis?
saq.a: Urgent echo: acute severe MR from posteromedial papillary muscle rupture (flail leaflet); the murmur can be soft because the LA pressure rises fast. Needs surgery.

cards.name: Sinuatrial nodal artery
cards.core: A small atrial branch that runs to the SA node at the SVC–RA junction; it explains why sinus node dysfunction can follow an RCA or LCx occlusion or atrial surgery.

quick.text: Runs over the atria to the **SVC–RA junction**, around the **SA node**
From the **proximal RCA** (≈ 60 %) or the **LCx** (≈ 40 %)
Occlusion or surgical injury → **sinus bradycardia, pauses, AF**
LCx-origin artery crosses the **LA roof**: at risk in some mitral approaches

anatomy.summary: A thin atrial branch, usually from the proximal RCA, that circles the SVC–RA junction to the SA node.
anatomy.detail: Usually the first or second branch of the proximal RCA; in the rest it comes from the proximal LCx and crosses the roof of the left atrium. It runs to the junction of the SVC and RA and often passes through the SA node, which is built around it. Small atrial branches leave it on the way.

function.summary: Feeds the SA node and nearby atrial muscle.
function.detail: The SA node lies just under the epicardium at the top of the crista terminalis, wrapped round this artery. Its blood supply keeps the pacemaker cells working.

supply.summary: Territory: SA node, crista terminalis region, parts of both atria.
supply.detail: Territory: the SA node, the region of the crista terminalis and parts of the RA and LA walls.

relations.why: The node is arranged around the artery; injury or occlusion stops or slows the pacemaker.
Surgery or ablation near the SVC–RA junction can injure the artery or the node itself.
An LCx-origin artery crosses here: superior transseptal or extended atriotomy incisions can cut it.

cut.text: The SA node region at the top of the crista terminalis (artery runs on the outside).

ecg.text: No direct sign; ischaemia shows as sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses or atrial arrhythmias.

complications.name: Sinus node dysfunction after MI
complications.mechanism: Proximal RCA (or LCx) occlusion takes out the SA nodal artery; the node becomes ischaemic.
complications.presentation: Sinus bradycardia or pauses, sometimes AF, in inferior MI; usually recovers.
complications.hook: Sinus brady/pauses in proximal RCA MI

complications.name: Side-branch loss during RCA stenting
complications.mechanism: A stent across the origin closes the SA nodal artery.
complications.presentation: New sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest or AF during or after PCI.
complications.hook: New sinus arrest or AF after RCA stent

complications.name: Sinus node injury in cardiac surgery
complications.mechanism: Atrial incisions or cannulation near the SVC–RA junction damage the artery or the node.
complications.presentation: Junctional rhythm or sinus node dysfunction after surgery; may need a pacemaker.

student.text: The SA node is fed by the RCA in about 60 % and the LCx in about 40 %, independent of dominance.
Sinus bradycardia in an inferior MI can be vagal or direct SA nodal ischaemia.

resident.text: Loss of the SA nodal or atrial branches can cause atrial ischaemia, AF or sinus arrest.
The SA nodal artery's origin does not follow dominance; the AV nodal artery does.

saq.q: Which arteries supply the SA node, and roughly how often?
saq.a: The SA nodal artery: from the RCA in about 60 % and the LCx in about 40 %.

saq.q: After RCA PCI the patient develops sinus arrest with a junctional escape. Explain the mechanism.
saq.a: The stent closed the SA nodal branch at its origin; the ischaemic SA node fails and a junctional pacemaker takes over.

cards.name: AV nodal artery
cards.core: A small branch from the U-turn of the dominant artery at the crux that runs up to the AV node; it is why inferior MI causes nodal block that usually recovers.

quick.text: Leaves the **crux** (U-turn of the dominant artery) and runs up to **Koch's triangle**
Feeds the **AV node** and proximal His; the **LAD septals** also feed the His
Inferior MI → **nodal block**: Wenckebach, narrow escape, usually transient
Anterior MI block is **infranodal**: wide escape, often permanent

anatomy.summary: From the crux, where the dominant artery makes a U-turn, upwards into the septum to the AV node.
anatomy.detail: At the crux the dominant artery (the RCA in about 80–90 %) loops in an inverted U. From the top of the loop the AV nodal artery runs upwards into the base of the atrial septum to the AV node at the apex of Koch's triangle.

function.summary: The main blood supply of the AV node.
function.detail: The compact AV node depends mainly on this artery. The His bundle and the start of the bundle branches also receive septal branches of the LAD, so they have two supplies.

supply.summary: Territory: AV node and proximal His bundle.
supply.detail: Territory: the AV node, the proximal His bundle and the nearby base of the atrial septum.

relations.why: The AV node at its apex is the target of this artery.
Give the His bundle a second supply, so infranodal tissue survives an inferior MI.
Lies near the crux and the base of Koch's triangle; slow-pathway ablation works in the same area.

cut.text: Koch's triangle: the AV node at its apex (the artery reaches it from below).

ecg.text: Ischaemia shows as PR prolongation, Wenckebach or complete block with a narrow junctional escape.

complications.name: AV block in inferior MI
complications.mechanism: Ischaemia of the AV node (plus vagal tone) slows or blocks conduction above the His bundle.
complications.presentation: First-degree block, Wenckebach or complete block with a narrow escape at 40–60 bpm; atropine often helps; usually resolves.

complications.name: Complete heart block at the node
complications.mechanism: Severe nodal ischaemia blocks all impulses; the junction below takes over.
complications.presentation: Narrow-complex escape at 40–60 bpm, usually haemodynamically tolerated.

student.text: Inferior MI: AV node (narrow escape, transient). Anterior MI: bundle branches (wide escape, dangerous).
The AV nodal artery comes from the dominant artery, the RCA in most people.

resident.text: Atropine removes vagal tone at the AV node, so it helps nodal block in inferior MI but not infranodal block.
Temporary pacing only for unstable or persistent block; most nodal blocks recover after reperfusion.

saq.q: Why is AV block in an inferior MI usually narrow-complex and temporary?
saq.a: Ischaemia of the RCA's AV nodal branch puts the block in the AV node; the His bundle below keeps its dual supply and gives a narrow escape, and the node recovers with reperfusion and less vagal tone.

saq.q: Compare AV block in inferior vs anterior MI: site, escape and need for pacing.
saq.a: Inferior: nodal block, narrow escape 40–60 bpm, atropine-responsive, usually transient. Anterior: infranodal (septal) block, wide escape, unstable, often needs pacing and may be permanent.

cards.name: Coronary sinus

parts.name: Coronary sinus ostium
parts.note: Opens into the RA between the IVC and the tricuspid valve, guarded by the Thebesian valve; forms the base of Koch's triangle.

cards.core: The large vein in the posterior AV groove that collects most cardiac venous blood and empties it into the RA; it is also a doorway for CRT leads and EP catheters.

quick.text: Runs in the **posterior left AV groove** and opens into the **RA** near the tricuspid valve
Collects the **great, middle and small cardiac veins**
**Dilated CS** behind the LA in PLAX → think **persistent left SVC**
Route for the **CRT LV lead**, EP catheters and retrograde cardioplegia
Its ostium forms the **base of Koch's triangle**

anatomy.summary: A short wide vein in the posterior left AV groove, from the GCV to its ostium in the RA.
anatomy.detail: It begins where the great cardiac vein ends (near the oblique vein of Marshall and the valve of Vieussens) and runs in the posterior part of the left AV groove, below the LA and above the LV. It ends at an ostium in the RA between the IVC and the tricuspid valve, partly guarded by the Thebesian valve. The middle and small cardiac veins join it close to the ostium.

function.summary: Drains most of the venous blood of the heart muscle into the RA.
function.detail: Collects venous blood from the LAD and LCx territories (great cardiac vein) and from the inferior wall and RV (middle and small cardiac veins). The rest drains through anterior cardiac veins and tiny Thebesian veins straight into the chambers.

supply.summary: Drains: LV (anterior, lateral, inferior), septum and part of the RV.
supply.detail: Drains: the great cardiac vein (anterior and lateral LV), the posterior LV vein, the middle cardiac vein (inferior wall, septum) and the small cardiac vein (right AV groove).

relations.why: Its ostium forms the base; the AV node lies at the apex and the slow pathway near the ostium.
Runs close to both: CS-based mitral devices can compress the LCx.
Lies under its floor; an unroofed CS opens into the LA (an atrial-level shunt).

echo.text: Small round vessel in the AV groove behind the mitral annulus, next to the descending aorta; dilated with a persistent left SVC.
Tilt the probe back: the CS runs along the floor of the LA into the RA.

cut.text: In the posterior AV groove under the LA.
The CS ostium below the fossa ovalis, at the base of Koch's triangle.
Behind the mitral annulus in the left AV groove.

ecg.text: No direct sign. EP studies use a CS catheter to record LA and LV activity.

complications.name: Persistent left superior vena cava
complications.mechanism: An embryonic left cardinal vein persists and drains into the CS, which enlarges.
complications.presentation: Usually no symptoms; dilated CS on echo; a left-arm bubble study fills the CS before the RA; complicates left-sided device implants.
complications.hook: Dilated CS; left-arm bubbles fill CS first

complications.name: Unroofed coronary sinus
complications.mechanism: Part of the wall between the CS and the LA is missing, so blood shunts from the LA into the CS and RA.
complications.presentation: Signs of an atrial-level left-to-right shunt (RV dilatation) with no defect in the fossa; often with a persistent left SVC.
complications.hook: Atrial shunt with an intact fossa

complications.name: CS injury during CRT lead placement
complications.mechanism: Dissection or perforation of the CS by the sheath or contrast injection.
complications.presentation: Contrast staining on venogram; rarely pericardial effusion or tamponade.

student.text: Most cardiac veins drain into the CS, which opens into the RA next to the tricuspid valve.
The commonest cause is a persistent left SVC; raised RA pressure is the other.

resident.text: The LV lead goes through the CS into a lateral or posterolateral branch, to pace the late-activating lateral wall.

resident.hook: Bubble study from the left arm
resident.text: Bubbles appearing in the CS before the RA prove a persistent left SVC.
A catheter in the CS records the LA and LV from the AV groove and is the reference for mapping left-sided pathways.

fellow.text: Slow-pathway ablation for AVNRT targets the area between the CS ostium and the tricuspid annulus, well below the compact AV node.

saq.q: Where does the coronary sinus run and where does it open?
saq.a: In the posterior left AV groove under the LA; it opens into the RA between the IVC and the tricuspid valve.

saq.q: A dilated coronary sinus is seen behind the LA on PLAX. What is the commonest cause, and how do you confirm it?
saq.a: Persistent left SVC. Inject agitated saline into a left arm vein: bubbles fill the CS before the RA.

saq.q: Why does a CRT LV lead go through the coronary sinus, and which branch is the target?
saq.a: It reaches the LV epicardium without entering the LV cavity. The target is a lateral or posterolateral vein, over the latest-activating lateral wall.

cards.name: Great cardiac vein
cards.core: The vein that runs up beside the LAD and then round the left AV groove with the LCx to become the coronary sinus; it drains the LAD and LCx territories.

quick.text: Starts near the apex beside the **LAD**, then turns into the **left AV groove** with the **LCx**
Drains the **anterior** and **lateral** LV into the **coronary sinus**
EP route: **LV summit** arrhythmias can be mapped from inside it
Its lateral tributaries are **CRT** lead targets

anatomy.summary: Begins at the apex as the anterior interventricular vein beside the LAD and continues round the left AV groove into the CS.
anatomy.detail: It starts near the apex, runs up the anterior interventricular groove beside the LAD (as the anterior interventricular vein), then turns left into the AV groove and runs with the LCx. Where the oblique vein of Marshall joins it, at the valve of Vieussens, it becomes the coronary sinus. On the way it receives the left marginal and other lateral veins.

function.summary: Drains the territories of the LAD and LCx.
function.detail: Carries the venous blood of the anterior wall, the anterior septum and the lateral wall to the coronary sinus.

supply.summary: Drains: anterior and lateral LV, anterior septum.
supply.detail: Drains: the anterior and anterolateral LV, the anterior septum (septal veins) and, through the left marginal vein, the lateral wall.

relations.why: Runs with it in the anterior groove.
Runs with it in the left AV groove and crosses over it, which matters for CS-based devices.
Becomes the CS at the valve of Vieussens.

cut.text: In the left AV groove next to the LCx (turn coronaries on).

complications.name: Ventricular arrhythmias from the LV summit
complications.mechanism: The LV summit, the top of the LV near the GCV, can be a source of PVCs or VT that is hard to reach from inside the LV.
complications.presentation: PVCs with an inferior axis and right-bundle or early transition pattern; mapped and sometimes ablated from the GCV.

complications.name: Compression of the LCx by a CS device
complications.mechanism: Where the vein crosses the LCx, a device placed in the GCV/CS can squeeze the artery.
complications.presentation: Lateral ischaemia after percutaneous mitral annuloplasty.

student.text: The GCV runs with the LAD then the LCx; the middle cardiac vein with the PDA; the small cardiac vein with the RCA.
At the valve of Vieussens, where the vein of Marshall joins.

resident.text: The LV lead aims at lateral or posterolateral tributaries of the GCV/CS, not the anterior vein (late activation is lateral).

resident.hook: Arrhythmias near the top of the LV
resident.text: PVCs from the LV summit may need mapping inside the GCV.

fellow.text: The oblique vein of Marshall joins the GCV at the start of the CS; ethanol infusion into it is used as an adjunct in persistent AF ablation.

saq.q: Which arteries does the great cardiac vein run beside, and where does it end?
saq.a: Beside the LAD in the anterior groove, then the LCx in the left AV groove; it ends by becoming the coronary sinus.

saq.q: Why is a CRT LV lead placed in a lateral rather than the anterior interventricular vein?
saq.a: In LBBB the lateral wall activates last; pacing there resynchronises the LV best. The anterior vein lies over the septum and anterior wall, which activate earlier.

cards.name: Middle and small cardiac veins

parts.name: Middle cardiac vein
parts.note: Runs with the PDA in the inferior interventricular groove and joins the CS near its ostium.

parts.name: Small cardiac vein
parts.note: Runs with the RCA in the right AV groove and joins the CS (or opens straight into the RA).

cards.core: Two veins on the inferior and right side of the heart: the middle cardiac vein beside the PDA and the small cardiac vein beside the RCA, both ending at the coronary sinus.

quick.text: **MCV**: inferior interventricular groove with the **PDA**
**SCV**: right AV groove with the **RCA**
Drain the **inferior wall**, **inferior septum** and part of the **RV** into the CS
**Posteroseptal pathways** may need ablation inside the MCV or a CS diverticulum

anatomy.summary: The MCV runs up the inferior interventricular groove; the SCV runs round the right AV groove; both join the CS near its ostium.
anatomy.detail: The middle cardiac vein starts near the apex and runs up the inferior interventricular groove with the PDA to join the coronary sinus just before its ostium. The small cardiac vein runs in the right AV groove with the RCA and the acute marginal and joins the CS (or sometimes opens directly into the RA).

function.summary: Drain the inferior LV wall, the inferior septum and part of the RV.
function.detail: They carry blood from the territory of the PDA and the RCA back to the coronary sinus.

supply.summary: Drain: inferior LV wall, inferior septum (MCV); right AV groove and RV (SCV).
supply.detail: Drain: the inferior LV wall and inferior third of the septum (middle cardiac vein); the RV and the right AV groove (small cardiac vein).

relations.why: The MCV runs beside it in the same groove.
The SCV runs beside it; ablation inside the SCV or MCV can injure the nearby artery.
Both join close to the ostium, near the posteroseptal region.

cut.text: Inferior groove beside the PDA (turn coronaries on).

complications.name: Posteroseptal accessory pathway
complications.mechanism: Some accessory pathways cross near the CS ostium, inside the MCV or a CS diverticulum.
complications.presentation: WPW pattern with a posteroseptal delta-wave axis (negative delta in II, III, aVF); ablation may need to be done inside the MCV.

complications.name: Suboptimal CRT lead position
complications.mechanism: An LV lead placed in the MCV paces the inferior septum, not the late lateral wall.
complications.presentation: Poor response to CRT (no improvement in EF or symptoms).

student.hook: Match each vein to its artery
student.text: MCV with the PDA, SCV with the RCA, GCV with the LAD and LCx.
They join the coronary sinus close to where it opens into the RA.

resident.text: Negative delta waves in the inferior leads suggest a posteroseptal pathway, which may lie in the MCV or a CS diverticulum.
Energy delivered inside the MCV or SCV can injure the adjacent PDA or RCA; check with angiography first.

saq.q: Which artery does the middle cardiac vein run with, and which with the small cardiac vein?
saq.a: Middle cardiac vein: the PDA in the inferior interventricular groove. Small cardiac vein: the RCA in the right AV groove.

saq.q: Why is an LV lead in the middle cardiac vein a poor CRT position?
saq.a: It paces the inferior septum and inferior wall, close to the earlier-activating septum, instead of the late-activating lateral wall, so resynchronisation is weak.

cards.name: Aortic root and ascending aorta

parts.name: Ascending aorta
parts.note: Tubular part from the sinotubular junction to the arch, inside the pericardium.

parts.name: Sinuses of Valsalva
parts.note: Three bulges behind the cusps; the coronaries arise from the right and left sinuses.

parts.name: Sinotubular junction
parts.note: The waist where the root meets the tubular aorta; its dilatation also causes AR.

cards.core: The first part of the aorta: the root holds the aortic valve and the coronary ostia in its sinuses, and its dilatation or dissection threatens the valve, the coronaries and life.

quick.text: Root = **annulus, 3 sinuses, sinotubular junction**; the coronaries leave the **right and left sinuses**
Its elastic wall stores systolic energy and keeps **diastolic flow** going (coronaries fill in diastole)
**Type A dissection**: tearing pain to the back, new AR, tamponade → emergency surgery
Measure in **PLAX** at the annulus, sinuses, STJ and ascending aorta
**Bicuspid valve** and **Marfan** dilate the root and ascending aorta

anatomy.summary: Annulus, three sinuses of Valsalva and the sinotubular junction, then the ascending aorta up to the arch.
anatomy.detail: The root runs from the aortic annulus (the hinge of the cusps) through three bulges, the sinuses of Valsalva (right, left and non-coronary), to the sinotubular junction (STJ). The right coronary artery leaves the right sinus and the left main the left sinus. Above the STJ the tubular ascending aorta rises inside the pericardium, to the right of the pulmonary trunk, to the arch.

function.summary: Holds the aortic valve and acts as an elastic reservoir that smooths flow into diastole.
function.detail: The sinuses give the cusps room to open without blocking the coronary ostia and help them close. The elastic wall stretches in systole and recoils in diastole (Windkessel effect), keeping pressure and flow up in diastole, when the coronaries fill. Stiffening with age raises pulse pressure.

supply.summary: Wall fed by its own small vessels (vasa vasorum); it gives off the coronary arteries.
supply.detail: The wall is nourished from the lumen and the vasa vasorum. The root is the origin of the right and left coronary arteries.

relations.why: Root dilatation pulls the commissures apart, so the cusps no longer meet (aortic regurgitation).
A dissection flap or a TAVI valve can block them; the RCA ostium is the one most often involved in type A dissection.
The ascending aorta lies inside the pericardium, so rupture causes tamponade.
Wraps round the front and left of the root.

echo.text: Root at the sinuses, STJ and proximal ascending aorta; measure in end-diastole.
Root in cross-section with the three cusps (Mercedes sign).
LVOT, valve and proximal root.

cut.text: Root and cusps opened from the LV side.
Root at the centre of the valve plane.

ecg.text: No direct sign; a dissection into the RCA ostium can mimic inferior STEMI.

complications.name: Type A aortic dissection
complications.mechanism: An intimal tear lets blood split the wall of the ascending aorta; the false lumen can extend back to the valve, the coronaries or the pericardium.
complications.presentation: Sudden tearing chest pain to the back, pulse or BP difference between the arms, new AR murmur, tamponade or stroke; sometimes inferior STEMI.
complications.hook: Tearing pain, arm BP gap, new AR

complications.name: Root aneurysm with aortic regurgitation
complications.mechanism: Weak media (Marfan, bicuspid aortopathy, ageing, hypertension) lets the root dilate and pull the cusps apart.
complications.presentation: Often silent; early diastolic murmur, wide pulse pressure; found on echo or CT.

complications.name: Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm
complications.mechanism: A weak sinus bulges and bursts, usually into the RV or RA.
complications.presentation: Sudden breathlessness with a continuous machinery murmur and heart failure.

student.text: The RCA leaves the right sinus and the left main the left sinus; the non-coronary sinus has none.
It stores energy in systole and releases it in diastole, keeping diastolic pressure (and coronary flow) up.
Severe tearing chest pain that radiates to the back, with unequal arm pulses, is dissection until proven otherwise.

resident.text: Stanford type A (ascending aorta involved) needs emergency surgery; type B is usually managed medically unless complicated.
A type A dissection can occlude the RCA ostium: check for dissection signs before giving antithrombotics.
Operate on the root or ascending aorta at about 5.5 cm, or 5.0 cm in Marfan or with risk factors (lower again in some genetic syndromes).

fellow.text: Echo measures the root leading edge to leading edge in end-diastole; CT measures inner to inner. Compare like with like over time.

saq.q: Severe tearing chest pain to the back, BP 160/90 in the right arm and 120/70 in the left. Diagnosis and why is the left arm lower?
saq.a: Aortic dissection: the flap or false lumen narrows the origin of the left subclavian artery, so the left arm pressure is lower.

saq.q: Why does dilatation of the aortic root cause aortic regurgitation?
saq.a: The cusps hang from the root; when it widens, the commissures move apart and the cusps can no longer meet in the centre.

saq.q: Inferior STEMI with a new early diastolic murmur and a wide mediastinum on CXR. What must you exclude before the cath lab, and how?
saq.a: Type A aortic dissection involving the RCA ostium: urgent CT aortography (or bedside echo for a flap, AR, effusion) before antithrombotic therapy.

Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy (great vessels)

cards.name: Aortic arch and descending aorta

parts.name: Arch branches
parts.note: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries.

parts.name: Descending thoracic aorta
parts.note: Behind the LA and left of the oesophagus; seen in cross-section on PLAX.

parts.name: Abdominal aorta
parts.note: Below the diaphragm, left of the IVC in the subcostal window.

cards.core: The arch gives the arteries to the head and arms and then becomes the descending aorta behind the heart; the narrow isthmus after the left subclavian is where coarctation and traumatic tears happen.

quick.text: Arch gives the **brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian**
**Isthmus** after the left subclavian, tethered by the **ligamentum arteriosum**
PLAX: **descending aorta** behind the LA; **pericardial fluid lies in front of it**
**Coarctation**: arm hypertension, weak delayed femoral pulses
Left **recurrent laryngeal nerve** hooks under the arch → hoarseness with a big arch or LA

anatomy.summary: The arch curves backwards over the left bronchus and the RPA, then descends left of the spine through the diaphragm.
anatomy.detail: The arch runs from the front of the trachea back to its left side, giving off the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid and the left subclavian arteries. Just beyond the left subclavian the isthmus is tied to the pulmonary trunk by the ligamentum arteriosum (the closed ductus). The descending thoracic aorta then runs behind the LA, left of the oesophagus, and passes through the diaphragm at T12 to become the abdominal aorta.

function.summary: Distributes blood to the head, arms and the rest of the body; its baroreceptors sense blood pressure.
function.detail: The arch carries aortic baroreceptors (vagus nerve) that help set blood pressure. The descending aorta supplies the chest wall, spinal cord (via intercostal arteries) and abdomen.

supply.summary: Its branches supply the head, arms, spinal cord and abdomen.
supply.detail: Arch branches: the brachiocephalic trunk (right subclavian and right common carotid), left common carotid, left subclavian. Descending branches: intercostal, bronchial and oesophageal arteries, then the abdominal branches.

relations.why: The descending aorta lies just behind it: in PLAX it marks where pericardial fluid stops and pleural fluid starts.
Joined at the isthmus by the ligamentum arteriosum (the patent ductus in a newborn).
Hooks under the arch; a dilated arch or LA can stretch it (hoarseness).
Passes under the arch.

echo.text: Round descending aorta behind the LA, below the AV groove.
Abdominal aorta beside the IVC in the subcostal window.

cut.text: Descending aorta behind the left atrium.

ecg.text: No direct sign; coarctation causes LV hypertrophy.

complications.name: Coarctation of the aorta
complications.mechanism: A congenital narrowing at the isthmus forces the LV to pump against high resistance above it and lowers flow below it.
complications.presentation: Arm hypertension, weak delayed femoral pulses (radio-femoral delay), rib notching on CXR, often a bicuspid valve.
complications.hook: Arm BP high, femoral pulses weak

complications.name: Type B aortic dissection
complications.mechanism: A tear beyond the left subclavian splits the descending aorta.
complications.presentation: Tearing back pain between the shoulder blades; limb, kidney or gut ischaemia if branches are cut off.
complications.hook: Back pain between the shoulder blades

complications.name: Traumatic aortic injury
complications.mechanism: A sudden deceleration tears the aorta at the isthmus, where the mobile arch meets the fixed descending aorta.
complications.presentation: High-speed crash; wide mediastinum on CXR; often fatal at the scene.

student.text: Brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian: right to left.
In PLAX, pericardial fluid sits in front of the descending aorta; pleural fluid extends behind it.
Hypertension in a young person: feel the radial and femoral pulses together for coarctation.

resident.text: About half of coarctation patients have a bicuspid aortic valve; screen for both.
Uncomplicated type B dissection: control heart rate and BP first (IV beta-blocker, then vasodilator); stent graft if complicated.

saq.q: How do you tell a pericardial from a pleural effusion in the PLAX view?
saq.a: By the descending aorta: pericardial fluid lies in front of it (between the aorta and the heart); pleural fluid extends behind it.

saq.q: A 19-year-old has BP 170/90 in the arms and weak, delayed femoral pulses. Diagnosis and site?
saq.a: Coarctation of the aorta, at the isthmus just beyond the left subclavian artery.

saq.q: In type B aortic dissection, why give a beta-blocker before a vasodilator?
saq.a: A vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and a steeper pressure rise (dP/dt), which extends the tear. Beta-blockade first lowers heart rate and dP/dt.

ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guideline
Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy (great vessels)
