cards.name: Pulmonary trunk and arteries

parts.name: Right pulmonary artery
parts.note: Long; passes under the arch behind the ascending aorta and SVC to the right lung.

parts.name: Left pulmonary artery
parts.note: Short; arches over the left bronchus; the ductus joins near its origin.

cards.core: Carries all the RV output to the lungs and splits under the aortic arch into the right and left pulmonary arteries; a saddle embolus lodges here.

quick.text: From the **RV** in front and to the left of the aorta, spiralling round it
Divides **under the arch** into the **RPA** (behind the ascending aorta) and **LPA**
**Saddle embolus** at the bifurcation → acute RV failure, shock
PSAX at the aortic valve shows the trunk and bifurcation; **PASP from the TR jet**
**Loud P2** = raised pulmonary pressure

anatomy.summary: Leaves the RV through the pulmonary valve, runs up and back to the left of the aorta and splits under the arch.
anatomy.detail: The trunk starts at the pulmonary valve, in front of and to the left of the aortic root, and spirals round it. Under the concavity of the arch it divides into the long right pulmonary artery, which passes behind the ascending aorta and SVC, and the shorter left pulmonary artery, which arches over the left bronchus. The ligamentum arteriosum ties the start of the LPA to the aortic isthmus.

function.summary: A low-pressure, high-compliance conduit for the whole cardiac output.
function.detail: It takes the entire RV output at about a fifth of systemic pressure (systolic ~15–30 mmHg). Its compliance keeps RV afterload low; when the pulmonary vessels stiffen or narrow, pressure rises and the RV must work harder.

supply.summary: Wall fed by vasa vasorum; the lungs receive oxygenated blood from the bronchial arteries.
supply.detail: The trunk and arteries carry deoxygenated blood; their walls are fed by vasa vasorum. Lung tissue gets its oxygenated supply from the bronchial arteries (from the aorta).

relations.why: Pressure overload of the PA is felt directly by the thin RV.
The trunk wraps round the root; the RPA runs under the arch.
Runs behind the trunk; a dilated PA can compress it in severe PH.

echo.text: Trunk, pulmonary valve and the bifurcation into RPA and LPA.
Tricuspid regurgitant jet for PASP (4v² + RA pressure).

cut.text: Pulmonary valve and the start of the trunk, in front of the aortic root.
RVOT leading up to the pulmonary valve.

ecg.text: Pulmonary hypertension: right axis, dominant R in V1, P pulmonale; acute PE: sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3, RBBB, T inversion V1–V4.

complications.name: Pulmonary embolism
complications.mechanism: A clot from the leg veins lodges in the pulmonary arteries; a large one at the bifurcation (saddle) blocks most flow, and the RV fails.
complications.presentation: Sudden breathlessness, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxia; shock with a large clot; dilated RV on echo.

complications.name: Pulmonary hypertension
complications.mechanism: Disease of the small pulmonary arteries, left heart disease, lung disease or chronic clots raise PA pressure.
complications.presentation: Exertional breathlessness, loud P2, raised JVP, oedema; dilated PA and RV.
complications.hook: Loud P2, dilated PA and RV

complications.name: Patent ductus arteriosus
complications.mechanism: The fetal duct between the aorta and the LPA stays open, shunting aorta to PA.
complications.presentation: Continuous machinery murmur under the left clavicle; LA/LV dilatation with a large shunt.

student.text: The PA carries the whole cardiac output at about a fifth of aortic pressure.
PASP ≈ 4 × (peak TR velocity)² + RA pressure (from the IVC).
A loud pulmonary component of S2 means high pulmonary pressure.

resident.text: Mean PAP > 20 mmHg at rest; pre-capillary if PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg and PVR > 2 Wood units.
On CT a PA diameter larger than the ascending aorta (ratio > 1) suggests PH.
Shock or hypotension = high-risk PE: reperfusion (thrombolysis, or catheter/surgical options).

saq.q: How do you estimate PA systolic pressure on echo?
saq.a: From the peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity: PASP ≈ 4v² + estimated RA pressure (from IVC size and collapse).

saq.q: Why does a large PE cause shock?
saq.a: The clot raises RV afterload suddenly; the thin RV dilates and fails, LV filling falls (septum shift, low RV output), so cardiac output falls.

saq.q: What haemodynamic values define pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension (2022)?
saq.a: Mean PAP > 20 mmHg, PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg and PVR > 2 Wood units, measured at right heart catheterisation.

cards.name: Superior vena cava
cards.core: Returns blood from the head, neck and arms to the top of the right atrium; the SA node sits at its junction with the RA.

quick.text: Enters the **top of the RA**, right of the ascending aorta
**SA node** lies at the **SVC–RA junction** along the crista
**SVC obstruction** (tumour, leads, lines) → swollen face and arms
**Sinus venosus ASD** sits at its mouth, often with an anomalous right upper PV

anatomy.summary: A short valveless vein from the junction of the brachiocephalic veins to the top of the RA.
anatomy.detail: Formed by the right and left brachiocephalic veins behind the right first costal cartilage, it runs down to the right of the ascending aorta and opens into the top of the smooth part of the RA (sinus venarum). The azygos vein joins it from behind. The right phrenic nerve runs on its lateral side.

function.summary: Carries venous return from the upper body; no valve guards its opening.
function.detail: Drains the head, neck, arms and upper chest (via the azygos). With no valve, RA pressure is transmitted straight up into the neck veins: that is why the JVP reflects RA pressure.

supply.summary: Drains the head, neck, arms and upper chest wall.
supply.detail: Tributaries: right and left brachiocephalic veins, azygos vein.

relations.why: Sits at the junction; SVC isolation or surgery near it can injure the node.
Runs along it: ablation inside the SVC can paralyse the right hemidiaphragm.
Lies just behind it; a sinus venosus defect lets it drain into the SVC or RA.

cut.text: Opening at the top of the RA, above the crista terminalis.

ecg.text: No direct sign. The JVP waves (a, c, v) are read through it.

complications.name: Superior vena cava syndrome
complications.mechanism: Compression or clot (lung cancer, lymphoma, pacing leads, lines) blocks return from the upper body.
complications.presentation: Swollen face and arms, distended non-pulsatile neck veins, headache worse on bending; collateral veins on the chest.
complications.hook: Swollen face and arms, fixed JVP

complications.name: Sinus venosus atrial septal defect
complications.mechanism: A defect at the SVC–RA junction, outside the fossa ovalis, usually with the right upper pulmonary vein draining to the right side.
complications.presentation: Signs of an atrial shunt (RV dilatation, fixed split S2) with an intact fossa on echo; often needs CT/MRI or TEE.

student.hook: Why the JVP shows RA pressure
student.text: There is no valve between the RA and the SVC and internal jugular vein, so RA pressure is transmitted straight up the neck.
The SA node lies at the SVC–RA junction, which is why sinus rhythm P waves point down and left.

resident.text: Aim the tip at the lower SVC or cavo-atrial junction (about the carina level on CXR).

resident.hook: Sinus venosus ASD is easy to miss
resident.text: TTE often misses it; suspect it with unexplained RV dilatation and look with TEE or MRI.

saq.q: Why does the JVP reflect right atrial pressure?
saq.a: No valve separates the RA from the SVC and internal jugular vein, so RA pressure is transmitted up the neck.

saq.q: Unexplained RV dilatation, intact fossa ovalis on TTE. Which defect should you look for, and with what?
saq.a: A sinus venosus ASD at the SVC–RA junction (often with anomalous right upper PV drainage); look with TEE or cardiac MRI/CT.

sources: ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guideline
Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy (great veins)
verify: Line tip at carina level on CXR

cards.name: Inferior vena cava

parts.name: Hepatic veins
parts.note: Join the IVC just below the RA; their Doppler pattern reflects RA pressure and TR.

cards.core: Returns blood from the lower body to the floor of the right atrium; on echo its size and collapse with a sniff estimate right atrial pressure.

quick.text: Enters the **floor of the RA**; the **Eustachian valve** guards its front edge
Subcostal IVC: **size + sniff collapse** estimate **RA pressure**
**Plethoric IVC** that does not collapse: tamponade, RV failure, severe TR
**Hepatic veins** join it just below the RA: systolic flow reversal = severe TR

anatomy.summary: A wide valveless vein that pierces the diaphragm at T8 and opens almost at once into the RA floor.
anatomy.detail: It runs up the right side of the abdomen behind the liver, receives the hepatic veins just below the diaphragm, passes through the central tendon at about T8 and opens into the lowest part of the RA. A fold, the Eustachian valve, lies along the front of its opening and continues towards the CS ostium.

function.summary: Carries venous return from the legs, abdomen and liver; its calibre follows RA pressure and breathing.
function.detail: On inspiration, falling chest pressure draws blood in and the IVC narrows; when RA pressure is high it stays wide. In the fetus the Eustachian valve steered oxygenated IVC blood across the foramen ovale.

supply.summary: Drains the legs, pelvis, kidneys, and the liver (hepatic veins).
supply.detail: Tributaries: common iliac, renal, gonadal (right), adrenal (right), lumbar and hepatic veins.

relations.why: Guards its front edge; a big one directs IVC flow to the fossa ovalis.
The strip of RA floor between its orifice and the tricuspid annulus: the flutter ablation line.
Congestion of the hepatic veins in right heart failure causes a tender liver and abnormal LFTs.

echo.text: Long axis 1–2 cm from the RA junction: diameter and collapse with a sniff.
IVC and hepatic veins entering the RA.

cut.text: Opening in the floor of the RA with the Eustachian valve.

ecg.text: No direct sign.

complications.name: Cardiac tamponade
complications.mechanism: Pericardial pressure raises RA pressure, so the IVC stays full.
complications.presentation: Plethoric IVC with < 50 % collapse, RA/RV collapse, pulsus paradoxus, hypotension.

complications.name: Right heart failure and congestive hepatopathy
complications.mechanism: High RA pressure is transmitted back to the liver.
complications.presentation: Raised JVP, tender liver, ascites, oedema; hepatic vein systolic flow reversal in severe TR.

complications.name: Volume depletion
complications.mechanism: Low RA pressure lets the IVC collapse almost completely.
complications.presentation: Small IVC (< 1 cm) that collapses fully; hypotension that responds to fluid.

student.text: Small IVC that collapses > 50 % with a sniff: RAP about 3 mmHg; dilated and < 50 %: about 15 mmHg; in between: about 8.
Inspiration lowers chest pressure, draws blood in and narrows the IVC.

resident.text: Positive-pressure ventilation distends the IVC, so the sniff rules do not apply.
Systolic flow reversal in the hepatic veins is a specific sign of severe TR.

saq.q: IVC 1.6 cm, collapses more than 50 % with a sniff. Estimated RA pressure?
saq.a: About 3 mmHg (range 0–5).

saq.q: Why does a large pericardial effusion make the IVC plethoric?
saq.a: Pericardial pressure raises RA pressure; venous return backs up and the IVC no longer collapses with breathing.

saq.q: Why can't you use IVC collapse to estimate RA pressure in a ventilated patient?
saq.a: Positive-pressure ventilation raises chest pressure in inspiration, distending the IVC whatever the RA pressure, so the sniff criteria are invalid.

sources: ASE 2015 chamber quantification (RA pressure from IVC)

cards.name: Pulmonary veins
cards.core: Four veins that bring oxygenated blood from the lungs into the back of the left atrium; muscle sleeves inside them fire the ectopic beats that start most atrial fibrillation.

quick.text: Two **right** and two **left** veins enter the **back of the LA**
**Muscle sleeves** inside the veins fire the **triggers of AF**
**Pulmonary vein isolation** is the cornerstone of AF ablation
Pulsed Doppler in a PV: **S, D and atrial reversal** waves reflect LA filling pressure

anatomy.summary: Four veins (right and left, superior and inferior) open into the smooth posterior wall of the LA.
anatomy.detail: Usually four: right superior, right inferior, left superior and left inferior, though common ostia and extra veins are frequent. The right veins pass behind the SVC and RA; the left veins lie next to the LAA. Atrial muscle extends 1–3 cm into each vein as a sleeve.

function.summary: Return oxygenated blood to the LA; their sleeves can fire on their own.
function.detail: Flow into the LA is in two waves: in ventricular systole (S, as the LA relaxes and the mitral annulus descends) and in early diastole (D, as the mitral valve opens), with a small reversal during atrial contraction (Ar). The sleeves have short refractory periods and abrupt changes in fibre direction, which favour triggered beats and micro re-entry.

supply.summary: Drain the lungs; the bronchial veins partly join them.
supply.detail: They carry oxygenated blood from the lungs; part of the bronchial venous blood drains into them too (a small normal right-to-left shunt).

relations.why: The left superior vein lies just behind its ridge (the 'coumadin ridge'), which can mimic thrombus.
Lies right behind the LA and the veins: ablation there risks an atrio-oesophageal fistula.
The right upper vein lies behind it; in a sinus venosus defect it drains to the right side.

echo.text: Right upper pulmonary vein entering the LA; pulsed Doppler for S, D and Ar.

cut.text: Four venous openings in the back wall of the LA.

ecg.text: Triggered PACs and AF; PV ectopy can give an inferior P axis (superior veins).

complications.name: Atrial fibrillation triggered from the veins
complications.mechanism: Rapid firing from the muscle sleeves sets off AF in a susceptible atrium.
complications.presentation: Irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves, palpitations, stroke risk.

complications.name: Pulmonary vein stenosis after ablation
complications.mechanism: Burns too far inside a vein scar and narrow it.
complications.presentation: Weeks to months after AF ablation: breathlessness, cough, haemoptysis, recurrent pneumonia on that side.

complications.name: Anomalous pulmonary venous return
complications.mechanism: One or more veins drain to the right heart (SVC, RA, IVC) instead of the LA.
complications.presentation: Signs of an atrial shunt (RV dilatation); often with a sinus venosus ASD.

student.text: Most AF triggers fire from muscle sleeves inside the pulmonary veins.

student.hook: Four veins, back of the LA
student.text: Two on each side enter the smooth back wall of the LA.

resident.text: Electrically isolating the veins (pulmonary vein isolation) is the cornerstone of AF ablation.
A blunted S wave with a dominant D wave (and a large Ar) suggests raised LA pressure, except in young people with normal hearts.

fellow.text: The oesophagus lies behind the posterior LA; limit energy there to avoid atrio-oesophageal fistula, which presents days to weeks later with fever and neurological signs.

saq.q: Where do most of the triggers for atrial fibrillation come from, and why there?
saq.a: From the muscle sleeves inside the pulmonary veins: short refractory periods and abrupt fibre-direction changes favour triggered beats and micro re-entry.

saq.q: Three months after AF ablation, cough, haemoptysis and breathlessness. Likely cause and test?
saq.a: Pulmonary vein stenosis from ablation scar; confirm with CT pulmonary venography.

cards.name: Crista terminalis
cards.core: A muscle ridge inside the RA between its smooth back and its ridged front; the SA node lies at its top, and it is a highway and a barrier for atrial conduction.

quick.text: Ridge from the **SVC** opening down to the **IVC**, separating smooth and ridged RA
Fast conduction **along** it, slow **across** it
**Focal atrial tachycardias** often start on it
A prominent crista can be mistaken for an **RA mass or thrombus**

anatomy.summary: A C-shaped muscle ridge on the inside of the RA, matching the sulcus terminalis on the outside.
anatomy.detail: It curves from the front of the SVC opening down the lateral RA wall to the front of the IVC opening. Behind it lies the smooth sinus venarum (from the embryonic sinus venosus); in front, the pectinate muscles fan out from it into the appendage. The SA node lies at its upper end, just under the epicardium.

function.summary: Conducts fast along its length and blocks conduction across it.
function.detail: Its fibres run lengthways, so impulses travel quickly along it but slowly across it (anisotropy). In typical flutter it forms the posterior wall of the circuit, forcing the wave round the tricuspid ring.

supply.summary: Branches of the SA nodal artery and RA branches of the RCA.
supply.detail: Mainly the SA nodal artery and atrial branches of the RCA (or LCx).

relations.why: Lies at its top; the sinus impulse runs down it.
Fan out from it into the RA appendage.
Together they channel the typical flutter circuit.

cut.text: The ridge on the lateral wall, from SVC to IVC.

ecg.text: Crista tachycardia: P waves resemble sinus P waves (upright in I and II, often negative in aVR, biphasic in V1).

complications.name: Focal atrial tachycardia from the crista
complications.mechanism: Automatic or triggered cells along the crista fire faster than the SA node.
complications.presentation: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia with P waves close to sinus in shape.

complications.name: Typical atrial flutter
complications.mechanism: The crista acts as a line of block, so a macro re-entry circles the tricuspid ring through the cavotricuspid isthmus.
complications.presentation: Sawtooth flutter waves in II, III, aVF at about 300/min, often with 2:1 block (ventricular rate about 150).

complications.name: Mistaken for an RA mass
complications.mechanism: A prominent crista bulges into the RA cavity on echo.
complications.presentation: Imaging pitfall; avoid needless anticoagulation or work-up.

student.text: Behind the crista the RA is smooth (sinus venarum); in front it is ridged by pectinate muscles.
The SA node lies at the top of the crista next to the SVC.

resident.text: Conduction is fast along the crista and slow across it, which helps make it a barrier in flutter.
A focal AT with near-sinus P morphology often comes from the crista; think of it in 'inappropriate sinus tachycardia'.

saq.q: What does the crista terminalis separate, and what lies at its top?
saq.a: It separates the smooth posterior RA (sinus venarum) from the ridged anterior RA with pectinate muscles. The SA node lies at its top.

saq.q: How does the crista terminalis take part in typical atrial flutter?
saq.a: Conduction across it is slow, so it acts as a posterior line of block; the wave circles the tricuspid ring and must pass through the cavotricuspid isthmus.

sources: Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy (right atrium)

cards.name: Pectinate muscles
cards.core: Comb-like muscle ridges in the atrial appendages and the front of the RA; the thin wall between them is easy to perforate, and they can mimic thrombus on echo.

quick.text: Ridges fan from the **crista** into the **RA appendage**; the **LAA** has them too
Thin wall between ridges: **lead or catheter perforation** risk
On TEE they can mimic **LAA thrombus**
Mark the part of the atrium from the **embryonic atrium**

anatomy.summary: Parallel muscle bands running from the crista terminalis into the RA appendage; finer ones line the LAA.
anatomy.detail: In the RA they arise from the crista and run forwards like the teeth of a comb into the broad, triangular right appendage. The LAA is long and finger-like with finer pectinate muscles. Between the ridges the atrial wall can be paper-thin.

function.summary: Add contractile muscle to the appendages without thickening the whole wall.
function.detail: They strengthen the appendage wall and add to atrial contraction. Their pattern also tells morphological right from left atrium, independent of where the chamber sits.

supply.summary: Atrial branches of the RCA and LCx.
supply.detail: Atrial branches of the RCA (right) and LCx (left).

relations.why: Their origin.
Contains finer pectinate muscles; slow flow there in AF forms clots.

cut.text: Ridges on the anterolateral RA wall in front of the crista.
Fine ridges inside the LAA.

ecg.text: No direct sign.

complications.name: Perforation by a pacing lead or catheter
complications.mechanism: The thin wall between ridges is pierced.
complications.presentation: Pericardial effusion or tamponade after device implant or ablation; chest pain, hypotension.

complications.name: Mistaken for LAA thrombus
complications.mechanism: A prominent pectinate ridge looks like a mass on TEE.
complications.presentation: Imaging pitfall; contrast or multiple views help decide.

student.text: Pectinate muscles make the front of the RA rough; the back (sinus venarum) is smooth.
The right appendage is broad and triangular; the left is narrow and finger-like.

resident.text: A thrombus moves independently and has a different texture; pectinate ridges are linear, move with the wall and are seen in several views.
Appendage shape and pectinate pattern identify morphological right and left atria in congenital heart disease.

saq.q: Where are the pectinate muscles found, and what makes the wall there risky for catheters?
saq.a: In the atrial appendages and the front of the RA; the wall between the ridges is very thin, so leads and catheters can perforate it.

saq.q: On TEE, how do you tell a pectinate ridge from LAA thrombus?
saq.a: Ridges are linear, move with the wall and appear in several views; a thrombus is a mass with independent motion, often with spontaneous echo contrast.

sources: Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy (right atrium)

cards.name: Eustachian and Thebesian valves

parts.name: Eustachian valve
parts.note: Crescent fold on the front edge of the IVC opening; its ridge continues as the tendon of Todaro.

parts.name: Thebesian valve
parts.note: Thin fold over part of the coronary sinus ostium.

cards.core: Remnant flaps at the openings of the IVC (Eustachian) and coronary sinus (Thebesian) in the RA; harmless alone, but they matter for PFO embolism and catheter work.

quick.text: **Eustachian**: front edge of the **IVC**; **Thebesian**: over the **CS ostium**
In the fetus the Eustachian valve steered IVC blood to the **foramen ovale**
A large Eustachian valve + **PFO** → paradoxical embolism risk
Eustachian ridge continues as the **tendon of Todaro**

anatomy.summary: Two thin flaps in the RA: one along the front of the IVC opening, one over the CS ostium.
anatomy.detail: The Eustachian valve is a crescent along the anterior edge of the IVC orifice; its ridge continues medially as the Eustachian ridge and the tendon of Todaro. The Thebesian valve is a thin fold over part of the coronary sinus ostium. A lace-like remnant (Chiari network) is found in some hearts.

function.summary: Fetal flow guides; little function after birth.
function.detail: Before birth the Eustachian valve directed oxygen-rich IVC blood across the foramen ovale into the LA. After birth both are remnants, varying from absent to prominent.

supply.summary: Atrial branches of the RCA.
supply.detail: Small atrial branches of the RCA.

relations.why: A large Eustachian valve keeps directing IVC flow to it, favouring paradoxical embolism through a PFO.
A big Eustachian ridge can make catheter contact on the CTI difficult.
A prominent Thebesian valve makes CS cannulation (CRT leads, EP) harder.

echo.text: Linear echo at the IVC–RA junction.
Thin echo in the RA near the IVC with an inferior tilt.

cut.text: Fold at the IVC opening and over the CS ostium.

ecg.text: No direct sign.

complications.name: Paradoxical embolism through a PFO
complications.mechanism: A prominent Eustachian valve channels IVC blood, and any clot in it, towards the fossa ovalis.
complications.presentation: Cryptogenic stroke in a younger patient with a PFO and a large Eustachian valve or Chiari network.
complications.hook: Stroke in a young patient with PFO

complications.name: Difficult CS cannulation
complications.mechanism: A Thebesian valve covers part of the ostium and deflects catheters.
complications.presentation: Failed or prolonged CRT LV lead placement.
complications.hook: CRT lead won't enter the CS

complications.name: Mistaken for thrombus or vegetation
complications.mechanism: A mobile flap or Chiari network moves in the RA.
complications.presentation: Imaging pitfall; rarely, true endocarditis of the Eustachian valve in IV drug use.

student.text: The Eustachian valve steered oxygen-rich IVC blood across the foramen ovale to the left heart.
Eustachian over the IVC, Thebesian over the coronary sinus.

resident.text: A lace-like Eustachian remnant; associated with PFO and atrial septal aneurysm. Not a thrombus.
The Eustachian ridge continues as the tendon of Todaro, one side of Koch's triangle.

saq.q: What did the Eustachian valve do in the fetus?
saq.a: It directed oxygenated blood from the IVC across the foramen ovale into the left atrium.

saq.q: Why might a large Eustachian valve matter in a young patient with a cryptogenic stroke?
saq.a: It channels IVC blood (and venous clot) towards the fossa ovalis, increasing the chance of paradoxical embolism through a PFO.

cards.name: Membranous septum
cards.core: The thin fibrous top of the ventricular septum just under the aortic valve; it is the commonest site of VSDs, and the His bundle runs along its lower edge.

quick.text: Under the **right and non-coronary cusps**, above the muscular septum
The **septal tricuspid leaflet** splits it into **AV** and **interventricular** parts
**His bundle** runs along its lower rim → **heart block** after VSD closure or TAVI
**Perimembranous VSD**: harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal edge

anatomy.summary: A small fibrous patch at the top of the ventricular septum, beneath the aortic valve and next to the central fibrous body.
anatomy.detail: It lies below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps, continuous with the central fibrous body. The hinge of the septal tricuspid leaflet crosses its right side, dividing it into an atrioventricular part (between LV and RA) and an interventricular part (between LV and RV). The penetrating His bundle runs along its posteroinferior edge, on the crest of the muscular septum.

function.summary: Closes the gap between the muscular septum and the aortic root; electrically inert.
function.detail: It is the last part of the septum to close in the embryo, which is why defects are commonest here. It conducts no impulses; the His bundle runs just beneath it.

supply.summary: No muscle to supply; nearby His is fed by the AV nodal artery and LAD septals.
supply.detail: Fibrous tissue with little blood supply; the adjacent His bundle has a dual supply (AV nodal artery and LAD septal perforators).

relations.why: Runs along its lower edge: VSD closure, TAVI or septal surgery can damage it.
Sits right above it; a perimembranous VSD can let a cusp prolapse (aortic regurgitation).
Continuous with it.

echo.text: Thin segment just below the aortic valve; perimembranous VSD jet towards the RV.
Top of the septum below the aortic valve.
Upper septum under the aortic root.

cut.text: Thin pale area under the aortic cusps.
Top of the septum next to the AV valves.

ecg.text: No direct sign; a large VSD causes LV (and later RV) hypertrophy.

complications.name: Perimembranous ventricular septal defect
complications.mechanism: The membranous septum fails to close, so blood shunts from the LV to the RV.
complications.presentation: Harsh holosystolic murmur at the left sternal edge; a large shunt causes heart failure in infancy and later pulmonary hypertension.

complications.name: Complete heart block after TAVI or VSD closure
complications.mechanism: A valve frame or device presses on the His bundle beneath the membranous septum.
complications.presentation: New LBBB or complete heart block with a wide escape after the procedure; may need a pacemaker.

complications.name: Gerbode defect (LV-to-RA shunt)
complications.mechanism: A defect in the AV part of the membranous septum connects the LV to the RA.
complications.presentation: High-velocity jet into the RA that can be mistaken for TR (and overestimate PA pressure).

student.text: Perimembranous VSDs are the most common type.
A small VSD has a high pressure gradient and a loud murmur; a large one may be quieter.

resident.text: A short membranous septum or a deep valve implant raises the risk of conduction block and a pacemaker after TAVI.
An LV-to-RA jet looks like severe TR with a very high velocity; do not read it as severe pulmonary hypertension.

saq.q: Why does a perimembranous VSD cause a holosystolic murmur?
saq.a: LV pressure exceeds RV pressure throughout systole, so blood flows through the defect from the start to the end of systole.

saq.q: Two days after TAVI, a new LBBB then complete heart block. Explain the anatomy.
saq.a: The His bundle and left bundle emerge beneath the membranous septum just below the aortic annulus; the valve frame compresses or injures them.

cards.name: Pericardium
cards.core: A tough sac around the heart with a thin film of fluid inside; inflamed, filled with fluid or scarred, it can stop the heart filling.

quick.text: **Fibrous** outer sac + **serous** layer (parietal and visceral)
**Pericarditis**: diffuse ST↑ with **PR depression**, no reciprocal changes (except aVR)
**Tamponade**: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds, **pulsus paradoxus**
Fluid in **PLAX** lies **in front of the descending aorta**; RA/RV collapse in tamponade
**Constriction**: Kussmaul sign, septal bounce, pericardial knock

anatomy.summary: A fibrous sac lined by a serous membrane whose inner (visceral) layer is the epicardium.
anatomy.detail: The fibrous pericardium is a tough outer sac fused to the diaphragm and the great vessels. Inside, the serous pericardium has a parietal layer lining the sac and a visceral layer (epicardium) on the heart, with 15–50 mL of fluid between them. Reflections round the great vessels form the transverse sinus (behind the aorta and PA) and the oblique sinus (behind the LA). The phrenic nerves run on its sides.

function.summary: Limits sudden dilatation, lubricates motion and couples the two ventricles.
function.detail: It lowers friction, keeps the heart in place and limits acute overfilling. Because its volume is fixed, filling of one ventricle affects the other (interdependence), which is what exaggerates breathing effects in tamponade and constriction.

supply.summary: Pericardiophrenic and internal thoracic branches; pain carried by the phrenic nerve.
supply.detail: Blood from the pericardiophrenic and internal thoracic arteries. The parietal layer is sensitive (phrenic nerve), so pericardial pain can refer to the shoulder tip and trapezius ridge.

relations.why: Run on its surface: pericarditis pain refers to the trapezius ridge; surgery can injure them.
In PLAX, pericardial fluid stops in front of it; pleural fluid extends behind it.
Lies inside the pericardium: a type A dissection can bleed into it (tamponade).

echo.text: Echo-free space behind the LV, in front of the descending aorta.
Best window for size, RV diastolic collapse and pericardiocentesis.
RA systolic collapse; respiratory variation of mitral inflow.

ecg.text: Pericarditis: diffuse ST elevation with PR depression (ST depression and PR elevation in aVR). Effusion: low voltage and electrical alternans.

complications.name: Acute pericarditis
complications.mechanism: Inflammation of the pericardium (often viral) irritates the epicardium beneath it.
complications.presentation: Sharp pleuritic chest pain, better sitting forward; friction rub; diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.

complications.name: Cardiac tamponade
complications.mechanism: Fluid under pressure compresses the heart, so the chambers cannot fill.
complications.presentation: Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad), pulsus paradoxus > 10 mmHg; RA/RV collapse on echo.

complications.name: Constrictive pericarditis
complications.mechanism: A stiff, scarred pericardium stops filling after early diastole.
complications.presentation: Raised JVP that rises on inspiration (Kussmaul), oedema, ascites; pericardial knock; septal bounce on echo.

student.text: Diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal ST depression (except aVR) favours pericarditis over STEMI.
Hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds suggest tamponade.
Pericarditis pain is sharp, worse lying flat and better sitting forward.

resident.text: An inspiratory fall in systolic BP > 10 mmHg: in tamponade the RV fills at the expense of the LV in a fixed space.
Echo shows the fluid and chamber collapse, but tamponade is a clinical diagnosis; drain an unstable patient now.
Constriction: septal bounce, respiratory variation, preserved or high septal e'. Restriction: thick or infiltrated muscle, low e'.

fellow.text: In constriction the septal e' exceeds the lateral e', the reverse of normal.

saq.q: How can the ECG help tell acute pericarditis from STEMI?
saq.a: Pericarditis: diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, no reciprocal ST depression (except aVR). STEMI: regional ST elevation with reciprocal depression.

saq.q: Name Beck's triad and the condition it suggests.
saq.a: Hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds: cardiac tamponade.

saq.q: Explain the mechanism of pulsus paradoxus in tamponade.
saq.a: In a fixed pericardial space, inspiration increases RV filling, which pushes the septum left and reduces LV filling; LV stroke volume and systolic BP fall by more than 10 mmHg.

cards.name: Epicardial fat
cards.core: Fat under the visceral pericardium that fills the grooves around the coronary arteries; on echo it can mimic an effusion, and in excess it is linked with coronary disease and AF.

quick.text: Fills the **AV and interventricular grooves** around the coronaries
An **anterior** echo-free space only = usually **fat**, not effusion
**Metabolically active**: linked with CAD and AF
**Lipomatous hypertrophy** of the IAS spares the fossa (dumbbell shape)

anatomy.summary: Fat between the myocardium and the visceral pericardium, thickest in the grooves and over the RV.
anatomy.detail: It lies directly on the myocardium with no fascia in between, beneath the visceral pericardium (epicardium). It is thickest in the AV and interventricular grooves, along the coronary arteries and veins, over the RV free wall and at the apex.

function.summary: Cushions the coronaries and acts as a local energy store and hormone source.
function.detail: It protects and supports the coronary vessels and stores fatty acids for the myocardium. It also releases inflammatory signals into the muscle and vessels beneath it, which may promote atherosclerosis and atrial fibrosis when it is excessive.

supply.summary: Shares the coronary microcirculation of the muscle below.
supply.detail: Fed by small branches of the coronary arteries, the same microcirculation as the myocardium underneath.

relations.why: Run inside it; surgeons dissect them out of the fat in bypass surgery.
Lies beneath the visceral layer; true effusion is between the visceral and parietal layers.
Fat can infiltrate it (lipomatous hypertrophy), sparing the fossa ovalis.

echo.text: Echo-poor band in front of the RV free wall, moving with the heart.
Fat over the RV in the subcostal view.

ecg.text: No direct sign.

complications.name: Mistaken for pericardial effusion
complications.mechanism: Epicardial fat is echo-poor and lies in front of the RV.
complications.presentation: Imaging pitfall: an anterior space with no posterior fluid is usually fat.

complications.name: Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum
complications.mechanism: Fat accumulates in the septum, sparing the thin fossa ovalis.
complications.presentation: Dumbbell-shaped thick septum on echo or CT; usually harmless, sometimes atrial arrhythmias.

student.text: A space in front of the heart alone is usually fat; a true effusion also collects behind the LV.
The main coronary arteries run in the grooves, buried in epicardial fat.

resident.text: More epicardial fat (on CT) is linked with coronary atherosclerosis and AF; it is an imaging marker, not yet a treatment target.
A thick septum that spares the fossa ovalis is fat, not a tumour; MRI or CT confirms fat signal.

saq.q: On PLAX you see an echo-poor space in front of the RV but nothing behind the LV. What is it most likely to be?
saq.a: Epicardial fat: an effusion would also collect behind the LV.

saq.q: A thick, dumbbell-shaped interatrial septum that spares the fossa ovalis. Diagnosis?
saq.a: Lipomatous hypertrophy of the interatrial septum: fat infiltrating the septum around, but not in, the thin fossa. Usually benign.

cards.name: Sinoatrial (SA) node
cards.core: The heart's natural pacemaker: a strip of cells at the SVC–RA junction whose resting voltage drifts up on its own, so it fires first and sets the rate.

quick.text: Under the epicardium at the **SVC–RA junction**, top of the **crista terminalis**
**Phase 4 drift** (funny current, If) makes it the **fastest clock**
Sinus P: **upright in I, II, aVF**, negative in aVR
**Sick sinus**: bradycardia, pauses, tachy-brady syndrome
**SA nodal artery**: RCA ≈ 60 %, LCx ≈ 40 %

anatomy.summary: A spindle-shaped strip under the epicardium where the SVC meets the RA, running down the crista terminalis.
anatomy.detail: It lies just under the epicardium in the sulcus terminalis, at the top of the crista terminalis, and is built around the SA nodal artery. It is about 1–2 cm long, larger than it looks on diagrams, and connects to the atrial muscle through exit routes along the crista.

function.summary: Generates each heartbeat through spontaneous phase 4 depolarisation; nerves tune the rate.
function.detail: Its cells have no stable resting potential. In phase 4 the funny current (If, through HCN4 channels) and calcium release slowly depolarise them to threshold; phase 0 is a slow calcium upstroke. The steepest phase 4 slope wins, so it overdrives slower pacemakers below it. Sympathetic tone steepens the slope (faster); vagal tone flattens it and hyperpolarises the cells (slower).

supply.summary: SA nodal artery, from the RCA in about 60 % and the LCx in about 40 %.
supply.detail: The SA nodal artery runs through the node; its origin does not follow coronary dominance.

relations.why: Runs through the node; RCA or LCx occlusion can stop it.
The impulse leaves down the crista.
Ablation or surgery at the SVC–RA junction can injure the node.

cut.text: Top of the crista terminalis at the SVC opening.

ecg.text: Sinus rhythm: every P upright in I, II and aVF, followed by a QRS, rate 60–100.

complications.name: Sinus bradycardia
complications.mechanism: Strong vagal tone, drugs (beta-blockers, calcium blockers), hypothyroidism or nodal disease flatten phase 4.
complications.presentation: Rate < 60 with normal P waves; fine in athletes and sleep, symptomatic if severe.

complications.name: Sinus arrest
complications.mechanism: The node stops firing for a while.
complications.presentation: A pause with no P wave that is not a multiple of the P–P interval; an escape beat may end it.
complications.hook: Pause not a multiple of P–P

complications.name: Sinoatrial exit block
complications.mechanism: The node fires but the impulse fails to leave it.
complications.presentation: A pause that is an exact multiple of the P–P interval.

complications.name: Tachy-brady syndrome
complications.mechanism: A diseased node and atrium alternate between AF or flutter and long pauses after they stop.
complications.presentation: Palpitations then dizziness or syncope when the tachycardia ends; often needs a pacemaker so rate control is safe.

student.text: It has the steepest phase 4 slope, so it reaches threshold first and resets all slower pacemakers (overdrive suppression).
If (HCN4) is a slow inward current that opens as the cell repolarises: it is what makes the node a clock.
The impulse spreads down and to the left, so the P wave is upright in II and negative in aVR.

resident.text: A pause that is an exact multiple of the P–P interval is exit block; one that is not is arrest.
Blocks If: slows the sinus rate without lowering BP or contractility (used in HFrEF and inappropriate sinus tachycardia).
In sinus node disease, pace when bradycardia or pauses clearly cause symptoms; asymptomatic slow rates need no pacing.

fellow.text: After overdrive pacing, a long corrected recovery time suggests sinus node disease, but the test has low sensitivity.

saq.q: Why is the SA node the heart's pacemaker rather than the AV node?
saq.a: Its phase 4 depolarisation is fastest, so it reaches threshold first and resets (overdrives) the slower AV junction and Purkinje pacemakers.

saq.q: What do sympathetic and vagal stimulation do to the SA node?
saq.a: Sympathetic (β1, cAMP) increases If and calcium currents, steepening phase 4: faster. Vagal (ACh, M2) opens potassium channels and reduces If: hyperpolarised, flatter phase 4, slower.

saq.q: A rhythm strip shows a pause exactly twice the P–P interval. Name it and the mechanism.
saq.a: Sinoatrial exit block (2:1): the node fires on time but one impulse fails to reach the atrium.

sources: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (cardiac rhythm)
Netter's Atlas of Human Anatomy (conduction system)

cards.name: Internodal routes (right atrium)

parts.name: Anterior route
parts.note: Runs forwards round the SVC; gives Bachmann's bundle to the left atrium.

parts.name: Middle route
parts.note: Runs through the interatrial septum to the top of the AV node (fast input).

parts.name: Posterior route
parts.note: Runs down the crista terminalis and Eustachian ridge to the back of the AV node (slow input).

cards.core: Preferential paths through right atrial muscle that carry the sinus impulse to the AV node; they are fast because of fibre direction, not because they are insulated cables.

quick.text: **Anterior, middle, posterior** routes from the SA node to the **AV node**
**Fibre orientation** makes them fast; they are **not insulated**
The **first part of the P wave** is right atrial activation
Feed the **fast** (septal) and **slow** (posterior) inputs to the AV node

anatomy.summary: Three classic routes (anterior, middle, posterior) through ordinary RA muscle from the SA node towards the AV node.
anatomy.detail: Textbooks name an anterior route (which also gives Bachmann's bundle), a middle route through the septum and a posterior route along the crista terminalis and the Eustachian ridge. They are bundles of well-aligned working muscle, not insulated tracts like the bundle branches; whether they are truly 'specialised' is debated.

function.summary: Carry the impulse quickly to the AV node so atrial activation finishes before the ventricles fire.
function.detail: Atrial muscle conducts at about 1 m/s, faster along the fibres. The right atrium activates first (the first half of the P wave), then the left through Bachmann's bundle and the septum. The impulse reaches the AV node about 30–40 ms after the SA node fires.

supply.summary: Atrial branches of the RCA and LCx, including the SA nodal artery.
supply.detail: Atrial branches of the RCA and LCx.

relations.why: The posterior route runs along it.
Leaves from the anterior route to the LA.
Part of the RA floor where the typical flutter circuit runs.

cut.text: RA septal and lateral walls between the SA node and Koch's triangle.

ecg.text: P wave: right atrium first (early P), left atrium last; normal P < 120 ms and < 2.5 mm in II.

complications.name: Typical atrial flutter
complications.mechanism: A macro re-entry runs round the tricuspid ring through the RA muscle and the cavotricuspid isthmus.
complications.presentation: Sawtooth waves in II, III, aVF at about 300/min; ventricular rate often 150 (2:1).

complications.name: Right atrial enlargement
complications.mechanism: A bigger RA takes longer to activate and generates more voltage early in the P wave.
complications.presentation: Tall P wave in II (≥ 2.5 mm, 'P pulmonale'), as in pulmonary hypertension or tricuspid disease.

student.text: The internodal routes are normal atrial muscle with aligned fibres, not insulated wires.
The early P wave is RA, the late P wave is LA.
A peaked P wave ≥ 2.5 mm in II suggests right atrial enlargement.

resident.text: A regular narrow tachycardia at about 150 is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise.
The septal (fast) and posterior (slow) inputs to the AV node are what make AVNRT possible.

saq.q: Are the internodal routes insulated tracts like the bundle branches?
saq.a: No. They are bands of ordinary atrial muscle whose aligned fibres conduct faster; there is no insulating sheath.

saq.q: Which part of the P wave reflects RA activation, and what P-wave change suggests RA enlargement?
saq.a: The first part. RA enlargement gives a tall peaked P ≥ 2.5 mm in II (P pulmonale).

sources: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (cardiac rhythm)

cards.name: Bachmann's bundle
cards.core: A thick band of atrial muscle across the roof of the atria that carries the sinus impulse quickly to the left atrium; when it fails, the P wave widens and AF becomes more likely.

quick.text: Crosses the **roof of the atria** behind the aorta, from the **SVC** to the **LAA**
Activates the **LA** quickly so both atria contract almost together
Block → **P ≥ 120 ms**; advanced: **biphasic P in II, III, aVF**
Advanced interatrial block → **AF and stroke** risk

anatomy.summary: A band of parallel muscle fibres crossing the front of the atrial roof, from the RA near the SVC to the LA and its appendage.
anatomy.detail: It runs in the interatrial groove behind the ascending aorta, over the front of the atrial roof, linking the RA near the SVC to the LA wall and the base of the LAA. It is ordinary atrial myocardium with highly parallel fibres.

function.summary: The main fast route from the right to the left atrium.
function.detail: Its aligned fibres conduct fastest of all atrial routes, so the LA starts activating within about 30–40 ms of the RA and the P wave stays under 120 ms. Other links (coronary sinus muscle, the fossa rim) carry the impulse when it fails.

supply.summary: Atrial branches, often from the SA nodal artery.
supply.detail: Atrial branches of the RCA or LCx, often from the SA nodal artery.

relations.why: Its end reaches the LAA region.
Lies just in front of it.
Without it, the LA activates late from below (via the CS), which gives a biphasic inferior P wave.

cut.text: Roof of the atria behind the aorta.

ecg.text: Partial interatrial block: P ≥ 120 ms. Advanced: P ≥ 120 ms and biphasic (+/−) in II, III, aVF.

complications.name: Interatrial block
complications.mechanism: Fibrosis or ischaemia slows or blocks conduction in the bundle, so the LA activates late or from below.
complications.presentation: Wide P (≥ 120 ms); advanced block gives biphasic inferior P waves and predicts AF and stroke (Bayés syndrome).

complications.name: Left atrial enlargement
complications.mechanism: A large LA takes longer to activate, prolonging the late P wave.
complications.presentation: Broad notched P in II (P mitrale) and a deep negative terminal P in V1, as in mitral stenosis.
complications.hook: Notched P in II, deep negative V1

student.text: Bachmann's bundle carries the impulse quickly to the LA so both atria contract almost together.
A P wave of 120 ms or more means slow interatrial conduction or a big LA.

resident.text: Advanced interatrial block (biphasic P in II, III, aVF) is associated with AF and embolic stroke.
A deep, wide negative P terminal in V1 (≥ 1 small box deep and wide) suggests LA enlargement.

saq.q: What is the role of Bachmann's bundle?
saq.a: It is the fast muscle bridge from the RA to the LA across the atrial roof, so the LA activates soon after the RA.

saq.q: P wave 140 ms, biphasic in II, III and aVF. Name it and its clinical meaning.
saq.a: Advanced interatrial block: Bachmann's bundle is blocked and the LA activates retrogradely from below. It is linked with AF and stroke (Bayés syndrome).

Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (cardiac rhythm)

cards.name: His bundle

parts.name: Bifurcation
parts.note: Where the His divides into the right bundle and the left bundle fan, on the septal crest.

cards.core: The only normal electrical bridge through the fibrous skeleton: it pierces the central fibrous body and splits into the bundle branches, so disease here causes sudden, dangerous block.

quick.text: Pierces the **central fibrous body**, runs under the **membranous septum**
**All-or-none** conduction: no gradual PR lengthening
Block below the node → **Mobitz II** or complete block with a **wide escape**
Injured by **TAVI**, valve surgery, VSD closure
**Dual** supply: AV nodal artery + LAD septals

anatomy.summary: Leaves the AV node, pierces the central fibrous body and runs on the crest of the muscular septum before it divides.
anatomy.detail: The penetrating part passes through the central fibrous body; the branching part runs along the crest of the muscular septum, just under the membranous septum and the non-coronary/right cusp commissure, then divides into the right bundle and the left bundle fan.

function.summary: Carries the impulse quickly from the AV node to the bundle branches; all-or-none behaviour.
function.detail: Fast sodium-dependent conduction (about 1.5–2 m/s), with no decremental slowing: it either conducts normally or fails. The His-to-ventricle time (HV interval) is normally 35–55 ms. An escape pacemaker in the His itself is narrow-complex; below it, escape is slow and wide.

supply.summary: Dual: AV nodal artery and septal perforators of the LAD.
supply.detail: The penetrating His gets the AV nodal artery; the branching part also gets LAD septal branches.

relations.why: The His is the only normal route through it.
Lie just above it: TAVI frames and VSD devices can compress it.
Above it; block in the node is usually benign, block in the His is not.

cut.text: Crest of the septum under the membranous septum and aortic root.
Apex of Koch's triangle, where it enters the fibrous body.

ecg.text: Infranodal block: Mobitz II (sudden dropped beats, fixed PR) or complete block with wide escape. HV interval needs an EP study.

complications.name: Mobitz II second-degree block
complications.mechanism: Intermittent all-or-none failure in the His or bundles.
complications.presentation: Constant PR, then a P wave suddenly not conducted; often wide QRS; risk of complete block.

complications.name: Complete heart block (infranodal)
complications.mechanism: Disease or damage of the His–Purkinje system stops all conduction.
complications.presentation: P waves and QRS dissociated; slow wide escape (20–40/min); syncope (Stokes–Adams).

complications.name: Block after TAVI or valve surgery
complications.mechanism: The frame or sutures injure the His and left bundle just under the annulus.
complications.presentation: New LBBB or complete block in the days after the procedure.

student.text: The fibrous skeleton insulates atria from ventricles; the His is the only normal way through.
Fixed PR with sudden dropped beats means His or bundle disease: pacemaker territory.
A slow wide escape comes from below the His and can stop without warning.

resident.text: Atropine speeds the sinus and AV node but not the His; in infranodal block it can worsen the ratio by sending more impulses to a failing His.
Pacing the His or left bundle area uses the native system for a narrow paced QRS.
HV ≥ 70–100 ms on EP study in syncope with bundle branch block supports pacing.

fellow.text: Fibres in the His are pre-destined to bundle branches, so pacing the His can correct some bundle branch blocks.

saq.q: Why is Mobitz II more dangerous than Mobitz I?
saq.a: Mobitz II is block in the His–Purkinje system (all-or-none, can progress suddenly to complete block with a slow wide escape). Mobitz I is usually in the AV node and benign.

saq.q: Why can the His bundle be damaged during TAVI?
saq.a: It runs just below the membranous septum under the aortic annulus; the valve frame presses on it and the left bundle.

saq.q: Complete heart block with a wide escape at 30/min. Why may atropine fail or worsen it?
saq.a: The block is infranodal; atropine acts on the SA and AV nodes, not the His–Purkinje system, and more atrial impulses can worsen conduction. Use pacing (transcutaneous then transvenous) or isoprenaline as a bridge.

cards.name: Right bundle branch

parts.name: Right bundle in the moderator band
parts.note: The RBB crosses the RV cavity inside the moderator band to the anterior papillary muscle.

cards.core: A thin cord down the right side of the septum that crosses to the RV free wall in the moderator band; block widens the QRS with an rsR′ in V1.

quick.text: Thin cord down the **RV septal surface**, then across in the **moderator band**
**RBBB**: rsR′ in V1, wide slurred S in I and V6
New RBBB: think **PE**, **anterior MI**, ASD
Bumped by a **right heart catheter** → transient RBBB; dangerous if LBBB already present
Mainly **LAD septal perforators**

anatomy.summary: A long, thin, insulated cord down the right side of the septum to the anterior papillary muscle, via the moderator band.
anatomy.detail: It continues from the His on the right side of the septum, runs under the endocardium (often deep in the muscle in its middle part) and crosses the RV cavity inside the moderator band to the base of the anterior papillary muscle, where it fans into the RV Purkinje network.

function.summary: Activates the RV; because the RV is thin, losing it changes the late QRS, not the start.
function.detail: Normally both ventricles activate together. In RBBB the LV and septum activate normally (initial QRS unchanged), then the RV activates late by slow muscle-to-muscle spread: a late rightward, anterior force (R′ in V1, wide S in I and V6).

supply.summary: Mainly LAD septal perforators, partly the AV nodal artery.
supply.detail: Septal perforators of the LAD for most of its length; its start shares the AV nodal artery.

relations.why: Carries it across the RV to the anterior papillary muscle.
Its blood supply: anterior MI can block it.
Stretch from pulmonary embolism or ASD strains it.

cut.text: RV septal surface and the moderator band.
Right side of the septum.

ecg.text: Complete RBBB: QRS ≥ 120 ms, rsR′ in V1–V2, wide slurred S in I and V6; secondary T inversion in V1–V2.

complications.name: Right bundle branch block
complications.mechanism: Block in the RBB delays RV activation.
complications.presentation: QRS ≥ 120 ms, rsR′ in V1, wide S in I and V6; often a normal variant, but new RBBB needs a cause.
complications.hook: rsR′ V1, wide S in I and V6

complications.name: Bifascicular block
complications.mechanism: RBBB plus left anterior (or posterior) fascicular block leaves one fascicle working.
complications.presentation: RBBB with left axis deviation (or right axis); risk of complete heart block, especially with syncope.

complications.name: Complete block during right heart catheterisation
complications.mechanism: A catheter bumps the RBB in a patient who already has LBBB.
complications.presentation: Sudden asystole or complete block on the table.

student.text: rsR′ ('rabbit ears') in V1 and a wide S in I and V6.
The septum and LV still activate normally, so the first part of the QRS is unchanged; only the end is wide.
PE, anterior MI, ASD, RV strain; it can also be a normal variant.

resident.text: Unlike LBBB, RBBB leaves ST elevation readable.
In LBBB, have pacing ready before a right heart catheter: bumping the RBB can cause complete block.

saq.q: Why is the first part of the QRS normal in RBBB?
saq.a: The septum (from the left side) and the LV still activate through the left bundle; only the late RV activation is delayed.

saq.q: Describe the ECG of complete RBBB.
saq.a: QRS ≥ 120 ms, rsR′ in V1–V2, wide slurred S in I and V6, often T inversion in V1–V2.
keys: Wide S in I and V6

saq.q: Sudden breathlessness, sinus tachycardia and new RBBB. What diagnosis must you consider and why does it cause RBBB?
saq.a: Pulmonary embolism: sudden RV pressure and stretch slow conduction in the thin, long right bundle.

cards.name: Left bundle branch

parts.name: Septal fascicle
parts.note: Mid-septal fibres that fire first, giving the left-to-right septal activation (septal q waves).

parts.name: Septal fascicle
parts.note: Mid-septal fibres that fire first, giving the left-to-right septal activation (septal q waves).

cards.core: A broad fan on the left side of the septum that activates the septum and LV; block widens the QRS, removes septal q waves and makes STEMI hard to read.

quick.text: A **broad fan** down the **left septal surface**, splitting into fascicles
Its **septal fibres** fire first: septum activates **left to right** (small q in I, V6)
**LBBB**: broad R in I, aVL, V6 with no q; deep S in V1
LBBB **hides STEMI**: use **Sgarbossa** criteria
LBBB + low EF + QRS ≥ 150 ms → **CRT**

anatomy.summary: A wide fan, not a cord, leaving the His under the aortic root and spreading down the left septal surface.
anatomy.detail: It emerges under the commissure between the right and non-coronary aortic cusps and spreads as a broad sheet down the left side of the septum, dividing into the anterior, posterior and (variable) septal fascicles, which reach the papillary muscles and Purkinje network.

function.summary: Activates the septum (left to right) and the LV quickly and in sync.
function.detail: Septal fibres fire first, so the septum depolarises from left to right: the small q in I, aVL, V5–V6 and the small r in V1. In LBBB the septum is activated from the right, the LV activates slowly from muscle to muscle, and contraction becomes dyssynchronous (the septum moves early, the lateral wall late).

supply.summary: Dual: LAD septal perforators and the PDA (RCA).
supply.detail: Its broad trunk gets LAD septal branches in front and PDA septal branches behind, so complete LBBB usually means extensive disease.

relations.why: Emerges just under it: TAVI and aortic surgery commonly cause new LBBB.
Spreads over its left surface.
Divides into the anterior and posterior fascicles.

cut.text: Fan on the left septal surface below the aortic valve.
Left side of the septum.

echo.text: LBBB: early inward septal 'flash' and late lateral contraction (dyssynchrony).

ecg.text: Complete LBBB: QRS ≥ 120 ms, QS or rS in V1, broad notched R in I, aVL, V5–V6, no septal q; ST–T opposite to the QRS.

complications.name: Left bundle branch block
complications.mechanism: Block in the main left bundle makes the septum activate from the right and the LV late.
complications.presentation: QRS ≥ 120 ms, deep S in V1, broad notched R in I, aVL, V6, no q; often with structural heart disease.
complications.hook: Deep S V1, broad R V6, no q

complications.name: LBBB-induced cardiomyopathy
complications.mechanism: Dyssynchronous contraction wastes work and the LV slowly dilates.
complications.presentation: Falling EF with LBBB and no other cause; improves with CRT or conduction system pacing.

complications.name: Hidden STEMI in LBBB
complications.mechanism: LBBB distorts the ST segment, masking ischaemic ST elevation.
complications.presentation: Chest pain with LBBB: concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm or excessively discordant ST (modified Sgarbossa) suggests occlusion.

student.text: The left septal fibres fire first, so the septum depolarises left to right: small q in I and V6, small r in V1.
Deep S in V1, broad notched R in I, aVL and V6, no q waves.
LBBB masks ST elevation; use the Sgarbossa criteria and the clinical picture.

resident.text: Concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm, concordant ST depression ≥ 1 mm in V1–V3, or discordant ST elevation ≥ 25 % of the S depth suggest acute occlusion.
Symptomatic HFrEF with EF ≤ 35 %, LBBB and QRS ≥ 150 ms despite therapy: CRT.
Common; follow up for progression to complete block.

fellow.text: Pacing the left bundle area can correct LBBB and is an alternative to biventricular CRT.

saq.q: Why is there a small q wave in I and V6 normally, and why does it disappear in LBBB?
saq.a: The left septal fibres fire first, activating the septum left to right (away from I and V6). In LBBB the septum is activated from the right, so the initial force points leftward and the q disappears.

saq.q: Describe the ECG of complete LBBB.
saq.a: QRS ≥ 120 ms, QS or rS in V1, broad notched R in I, aVL, V5–V6, no septal q, ST–T opposite to the QRS.
keys: Broad notched R in V6, no q

saq.q: Chest pain, known LBBB, 2 mm concordant ST elevation in V5. What does it mean?
saq.a: Concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm meets Sgarbossa/modified Sgarbossa criteria for acute coronary occlusion: activate the cath lab.

verify: CRT class I criteria (QRS ≥ 150 ms, LBBB, EF ≤ 35 %)

cards.name: Left anterior fascicle
cards.core: A thin, long branch of the left bundle to the anterolateral papillary muscle; it is the most often blocked fascicle and its block swings the axis far to the left.

quick.text: Runs **up and forwards** to the **anterolateral papillary muscle**
**LAFB**: axis ≤ −45°, **qR in aVL**, rS in II, III, aVF
**Thin + single supply** → the commonest fascicular block
RBBB + LAFB = **bifascicular block**

anatomy.summary: A thin fascicle running anterosuperiorly across the left septal surface to the anterolateral papillary muscle.
anatomy.detail: It leaves the left bundle and runs up and forwards towards the base of the anterolateral papillary muscle, branching into the Purkinje network of the anterior and lateral LV.

function.summary: Activates the anterior and upper lateral LV.
function.detail: With it blocked, the LV activates first from the posterior fascicle (inferior wall), then upwards and leftwards: the main QRS force points up and left (left axis deviation) with little widening.

supply.summary: LAD septal perforators only.
supply.detail: Septal branches of the LAD, so anterior MI can block it.

relations.why: Its target.
Single blood supply.
Shares the LAD supply, so they often fail together (bifascicular block).

cut.text: Upper left septal surface towards the anterolateral papillary muscle.

ecg.text: LAFB: axis −45° or more negative, qR in I and aVL, rS in II, III, aVF, QRS < 120 ms.

complications.name: Left anterior fascicular block
complications.mechanism: The thin fascicle fails, often from fibrosis, hypertension or anterior MI.
complications.presentation: Left axis deviation (≤ −45°), qR in aVL, rS in the inferior leads.

complications.name: Bifascicular block (RBBB + LAFB)
complications.mechanism: Only the posterior fascicle still conducts.
complications.presentation: RBBB with left axis deviation; with syncope, consider complete heart block.

student.text: It is thin, long and has a single (LAD) supply.
LAFB swings the axis to −45° or beyond, with qR in aVL.

resident.text: Before calling LAFB, exclude inferior MI (Q waves in II, III, aVF) as a cause of left axis.
Bifascicular block with unexplained syncope: EP study or ambulatory monitoring; pacing if HV is prolonged or block is caught.

saq.q: Why is the left anterior fascicle the most commonly blocked?
saq.a: It is thin and long and has a single blood supply from LAD septal branches.

saq.q: ECG: QRS 150 ms with rsR′ in V1, axis −60°. Name the pattern and its risk.
saq.a: Bifascicular block (RBBB + LAFB); only the left posterior fascicle conducts, so there is a risk of complete heart block, especially with syncope.

cards.name: Left posterior fascicle
cards.core: A short, broad branch of the left bundle to the posteromedial papillary muscle; because it is broad and doubly supplied, isolated block is rare and means extensive disease.

quick.text: Short and broad, **down and back** to the **posteromedial papillary muscle**
**LPFB**: right axis (> +90°), **rS in I/aVL**, qR in III/aVF
Rare: **exclude RVH, lateral MI, thin build** first
Origin of **fascicular VT** (RBBB + left axis, verapamil-sensitive)

anatomy.summary: A short, broad fan running down and back over the left septal surface to the posteromedial papillary muscle.
anatomy.detail: It leaves the left bundle as a wide band and spreads inferiorly and posteriorly to the base of the posteromedial papillary muscle and the inferior LV Purkinje network.

function.summary: Activates the inferior and posterior LV.
function.detail: With it blocked, the LV activates first from the anterior fascicle (upper wall), then downwards and rightwards: right axis deviation.

supply.summary: Dual: LAD septal perforators and the PDA.
supply.detail: Supplied by LAD septal branches and PDA septal branches; this, and its width, protect it.

relations.why: Its target.
Part of its dual supply.

cut.text: Lower left septal surface towards the posteromedial papillary muscle.

ecg.text: LPFB: axis > +90°, rS in I and aVL, qR in III and aVF, QRS < 120 ms, after excluding RVH and lateral MI.

complications.name: Left posterior fascicular block
complications.mechanism: Extensive septal disease blocks even this broad fascicle.
complications.presentation: Right axis deviation with rS in I and aVL; with RBBB it is a high-risk bifascicular block.
complications.hook: Right axis, rS in I and aVL

complications.name: Idiopathic fascicular VT
complications.mechanism: Re-entry in the Purkinje fibres of the posterior fascicle.
complications.presentation: Young patient with a regular wide tachycardia, RBBB pattern and left axis; stops with IV verapamil.

student.text: Broad and doubly supplied, so isolated LPFB is rare.
Before calling LPFB, exclude RVH, lateral MI, PE and a thin, vertical heart.

resident.text: Means only the anterior fascicle remains; high risk of complete heart block.
Fascicular VT (RBBB + left axis) in a structurally normal heart responds to verapamil; do not assume SVT with aberrancy.

saq.q: Why is isolated left posterior fascicular block rare?
saq.a: The fascicle is short and broad and has a dual blood supply (LAD and PDA).

saq.q: A 25-year-old has a regular wide tachycardia with RBBB pattern and left axis, normal echo. Likely diagnosis and drug?
saq.a: Idiopathic left fascicular VT (posterior fascicle re-entry); IV verapamil usually terminates it.

cards.name: Purkinje network
cards.core: A fast-conducting mesh under the endocardium that spreads the impulse through both ventricles within milliseconds; its cells also trigger PVCs and some ventricular fibrillation.

quick.text: Mesh under the **endocardium** at the ends of the bundle branches
Fastest conduction → both ventricles activate within **~ 80–100 ms**
Purkinje triggers start **PVCs, VF storms** after MI
Longest action potential → prone to **EADs** (torsades)

anatomy.summary: A subendocardial network at the ends of the bundle branches, including false tendons that cross the LV cavity.
anatomy.detail: Purkinje fibres spread from the bundle branches over the endocardium of both ventricles, mostly in the lower two thirds, and enter the working muscle through transitional cells. Free-running strands (false tendons) cross the LV cavity.

function.summary: Spreads activation almost simultaneously through the endocardium; activation then moves endocardium to epicardium.
function.detail: Purkinje fibres conduct at 2–4 m/s (large, fast sodium current and many gap junctions), so the whole endocardium activates within a few tens of milliseconds and the normal QRS is narrow (< 120 ms). Muscle then conducts outwards at about 0.5–1 m/s. As a pacemaker they are slow (20–40/min) and normally suppressed.

supply.summary: Bathed by cavity blood and fed by the overlying coronary branches.
supply.detail: Subendocardial Purkinje fibres partly get oxygen straight from cavity blood, so they often survive an infarct and can then trigger arrhythmias.

relations.why: Its source.
Activated early through Purkinje fibres so the valves are held before ventricular pressure rises.

cut.text: Fine network on the endocardium of both ventricles.

ecg.text: A narrow QRS (< 120 ms) means activation used the Purkinje system; a beat that starts in the muscle is wide.

complications.name: Premature ventricular contractions
complications.mechanism: An ectopic focus (often Purkinje or outflow tract) fires early; the beat spreads slowly through muscle.
complications.presentation: Early wide QRS without a P wave, then a compensatory pause.

complications.name: Purkinje-triggered VF or electrical storm
complications.mechanism: Surviving Purkinje fibres at the edge of an infarct fire early beats that trigger VF.
complications.presentation: Recurrent VF days after MI, each started by the same short-coupled PVC; ablation of the trigger can stop it.
complications.hook: Recurrent VF from the same PVC

complications.name: Torsades de pointes
complications.mechanism: A long QT lengthens the already long Purkinje action potential; early afterdepolarisations fire.
complications.presentation: Polymorphic VT twisting round the baseline after a long QT.

student.text: Purkinje fibres conduct about 3–4 times faster than muscle, so both ventricles activate together.
A beat that starts in the muscle (PVC, paced, BBB) spreads slowly and is wide.

resident.text: Purkinje fibres fed from the cavity survive MI and can trigger VF storms; target them with ablation if drugs fail.
The longest action potential in the heart makes Purkinje cells the source of EADs and torsades.

saq.q: Why is a normal QRS narrow but a PVC wide?
saq.a: Normally activation spreads through the fast Purkinje network (2–4 m/s); a PVC starts in the muscle and spreads slowly cell to cell (about 0.5–1 m/s).

saq.q: Recurrent VF three days after a large MI, each episode starting with the same short-coupled PVC. Mechanism and option?
saq.a: Triggers from surviving Purkinje fibres at the infarct border. Treat ischaemia and electrolytes, antiarrhythmics (amiodarone), sedation; catheter ablation of the triggering PVC if storms continue.

sources: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (conduction)

cards.name: Accessory pathway (left lateral)
cards.core: A strand of muscle that bridges the AV ring outside the AV node; it pre-excites the ventricles (WPW) and can carry re-entrant tachycardias, or AF at dangerous rates.

quick.text: Bridges the **mitral annulus** (left lateral), bypassing the **AV node**
**WPW**: short PR, **delta wave**, wide QRS
**Pre-excited AF**: irregular wide fast QRS; **avoid AV-node blockers**
**Ablation** cures it

anatomy.summary: A thin strand of working muscle crossing the AV groove; this model shows a left lateral pathway across the mitral annulus.
anatomy.detail: Accessory pathways form where the fibrous AV ring failed to insulate fully during development. They can sit anywhere round the mitral or tricuspid annulus; left free wall pathways are the most common.

function.summary: Conducts fast, without the AV node's delay, and can complete a re-entry circuit.
function.detail: Its sodium-dependent muscle conducts quickly and non-decrementally. In sinus rhythm the ventricle near it activates early (delta wave, short PR) and the rest via the normal system (fusion). It can form a circuit with the AV node: down the node, up the pathway (orthodromic AVRT, narrow) or the reverse (antidromic, wide).

supply.summary: Not applicable (a strand of ordinary muscle).
supply.detail: It shares the blood supply of the surrounding AV groove muscle.

relations.why: A left lateral pathway crosses it.
The other half of the AVRT circuit.
Used to map left-sided pathways; posteroseptal pathways can lie inside it.

cut.text: Across the left AV groove at the mitral annulus.

ecg.text: WPW: PR < 120 ms, delta wave, QRS > 110–120 ms, secondary ST–T change. Delta-wave polarity localises the pathway.

complications.name: Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome
complications.mechanism: Pre-excitation plus re-entry through the pathway and the AV node.
complications.presentation: Short PR and delta wave in sinus rhythm; episodes of regular narrow tachycardia (orthodromic AVRT).

complications.name: Pre-excited atrial fibrillation
complications.mechanism: AF impulses race down the pathway, which has no AV-node delay.
complications.presentation: Irregular, very fast, wide QRS of changing shape; can degenerate into VF.

student.text: Short PR (< 120 ms), delta wave and a wide QRS.
The pathway skips the AV-node delay, so the ventricle starts early.

resident.hook: Never block the node in pre-excited AF
resident.text: AV-node blockers (adenosine, verapamil, digoxin, beta-blockers) can push more impulses down the pathway and cause VF. Unstable: DC cardioversion; stable: procainamide or ibutilide; then ablation.
Narrow regular tachycardia, down the node and up the pathway; vagal manoeuvres or adenosine are fine here.

fellow.text: Shortest pre-excited R–R interval in AF ≤ 250 ms marks a high-risk pathway.

saq.q: Why does WPW cause a short PR interval and a delta wave?
saq.a: The pathway bypasses the AV-node delay, so part of the ventricle activates early through slow muscle-to-muscle spread (delta wave) before the normal system takes over.

saq.q: Irregular wide-complex tachycardia at 250/min with changing QRS shapes in a young man with WPW. What must you avoid and what do you give?
saq.a: Avoid AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, digoxin, beta-blockers). If unstable: DC cardioversion; if stable: procainamide or ibutilide; then ablation.

verify: Left free wall as the commonest site

cards.name: Cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI)
cards.core: The strip of RA floor between the IVC and the tricuspid annulus; the typical flutter circuit must pass through it, so a line of ablation across it cures typical flutter.

quick.text: RA floor between the **IVC** and the **tricuspid annulus**
Slow conduction here holds the **typical flutter** circuit together
Typical flutter: **negative sawtooth in II, III, aVF**, positive in V1
**CTI ablation** with bidirectional block cures typical flutter
The **RCA** runs close to its lateral end

anatomy.summary: A band of RA floor bounded by the IVC opening and Eustachian ridge behind and the tricuspid annulus in front.
anatomy.detail: It runs from the IVC orifice to the hinge of the posterior and septal tricuspid leaflets, below the coronary sinus ostium. Its surface is uneven: pouches, pectinate ridges and the Eustachian ridge can make catheter contact difficult. The RCA runs in the AV groove near its lateral end.

function.summary: A narrow, slow-conducting gate in the right atrial circuit round the tricuspid ring.
function.detail: The crista terminalis behind and the tricuspid annulus in front act as barriers, so a wave circling the tricuspid ring must pass through the isthmus. In typical flutter it goes up the septum and down the lateral wall (counter-clockwise viewed from the ventricle) at about 300/min.

supply.summary: RA branches of the RCA.
supply.detail: Atrial branches of the RCA.

relations.why: Its anterior boundary.
Its posterior boundary; a big Eustachian ridge makes ablation harder.
Runs near the lateral isthmus: deep lesions there can injure it.

cut.text: Floor of the RA between the IVC opening and the tricuspid valve.

ecg.text: Typical (counter-clockwise) flutter: negative sawtooth flutter waves in II, III, aVF, positive in V1, at about 300/min.

complications.name: Typical atrial flutter
complications.mechanism: A macro re-entry circles the tricuspid annulus and passes through the isthmus.
complications.presentation: Sawtooth waves in II, III, aVF at about 300/min; often 2:1 block giving a regular rate of about 150; clot risk as in AF.

complications.name: Flutter with 1:1 conduction
complications.mechanism: Class IC drugs slow the flutter rate so the AV node can conduct every wave.
complications.presentation: Very fast wide-complex tachycardia; give an AV-node blocker with IC drugs.

student.text: A regular narrow tachycardia at about 150 bpm is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise.
Look in II, III, aVF; adenosine can slow the ventricular rate and unmask them.

resident.text: A CTI line with bidirectional block cures typical flutter in over 90 %; anticoagulate as for AF.
Flecainide or propafenone can slow flutter to a rate the AV node conducts 1:1; always combine with an AV-node blocker.

saq.q: Regular narrow tachycardia at exactly 150/min. What should you suspect and how can you reveal it?
saq.a: Atrial flutter with 2:1 block; look for sawtooth waves in II, III, aVF, and give adenosine or vagal manoeuvres to slow AV conduction and unmask them.

saq.q: Why does ablation across the cavotricuspid isthmus cure typical flutter?
saq.a: The flutter circuit circles the tricuspid annulus and must pass through the isthmus; a complete line of block there interrupts the circuit.

cards.name: Koch's triangle

parts.name: Tendon of Todaro
parts.note: Fibrous cord from the Eustachian ridge to the central fibrous body: the upper border.

parts.name: Tendon of Todaro
parts.note: Fibrous cord from the Eustachian ridge to the central fibrous body: the upper border.

parts.name: Septal tricuspid hinge
parts.note: Attachment of the septal leaflet: the lower border.

parts.name: Compact AV node
parts.note: At the apex, next to the central fibrous body.

cards.core: A triangle on the RA septal wall that marks where the AV node lies; its apex holds the compact node and its base the slow pathway, the target of AVNRT ablation.

quick.text: Bounded by the **tendon of Todaro**, **septal tricuspid hinge** and **CS ostium**
**Compact AV node** at the **apex**, then the His enters the fibrous body
**Slow pathway** near the **base** (CS ostium): AVNRT ablation site
Ablating towards the apex risks **complete heart block**

anatomy.summary: A triangle on the RA septal wall: tendon of Todaro above, septal tricuspid leaflet hinge below, CS ostium at the base.
anatomy.detail: The tendon of Todaro (a fibrous continuation of the Eustachian ridge) runs to the central fibrous body; the hinge of the septal tricuspid leaflet runs below it; the coronary sinus ostium closes the base. The compact AV node lies near the apex, where the two sides meet at the central fibrous body; the His bundle enters the fibrous body there.

function.summary: A map for finding the AV node and its fast and slow inputs.
function.detail: The fast pathway enters the node from above (the septum near the apex); the slow pathway runs along the base near the CS ostium. In AVNRT these two form a circuit. Ablating the slow pathway at the base stops AVNRT while sparing the compact node at the apex.

supply.summary: AV nodal artery, from the crux.
supply.detail: The AV nodal artery reaches the node from below, coming up from the crux.

relations.why: Lies at its apex.
Its base; slow-pathway ablation is done just in front of it.
The apex meets it, where the His penetrates.

cut.text: RA septal wall: tendon of Todaro, septal leaflet hinge and the CS ostium.

ecg.text: AVNRT: regular narrow tachycardia with retrograde P buried in or just after the QRS (pseudo-r′ in V1, pseudo-S in II).

complications.name: AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT)
complications.mechanism: A circuit forms between the slow and fast pathways in Koch's triangle: down the slow, up the fast (typical).
complications.presentation: Sudden regular palpitations at 150–250/min; P waves hidden or a pseudo-r′ in V1; stops with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine.

complications.name: AV block from ablation or surgery
complications.mechanism: Energy or sutures near the apex of the triangle injure the compact node or His.
complications.presentation: Complete heart block after AVNRT ablation, ASD repair or tricuspid surgery; may need a pacemaker.

student.text: The compact AV node sits at the apex of Koch's triangle, near the central fibrous body.
Tendon of Todaro, septal tricuspid leaflet hinge, coronary sinus ostium.

resident.text: Slow-pathway ablation is done at the base near the CS ostium; moving towards the apex raises the risk of AV block.
In typical AVNRT the retrograde P wave falls at the end of the QRS: pseudo-r′ in V1 and pseudo-S in II, III, aVF.

fellow.text: Accelerated junctional beats during slow-pathway ablation are a sign of a good site; fast junctional rhythm with VA block warns of injury to the node.

saq.q: Name the three borders of Koch's triangle and what lies at its apex.
saq.a: Tendon of Todaro, the hinge of the septal tricuspid leaflet and the coronary sinus ostium (base). The compact AV node lies at the apex.

saq.q: Where is AVNRT ablated, and why there rather than at the apex?
saq.a: At the slow pathway near the base of the triangle (in front of the CS ostium). The compact AV node and His are at the apex; ablating there would cause complete heart block.
